title: Chapter 17
paragraphs: Stepan Arkadyevitch went upstairs with his pocket bulging from the bills the merchant had paid him three months in advance. The forest deal was finished, the money was in his pocket, the shooting had gone splendidly, and Stepan Arkadyevitch was in the cheeriest possible mood — which is exactly why he was so eager to dispel the gloom that had come over Levin. He wanted to end the day at supper as pleasantly as it had begun.
Levin was indeed out of sorts, and try as he might to be warm and welcoming to his charming guest, he couldn't shake his mood. The news that Kitty wasn't married had slowly begun to intoxicate him.

Kitty was unmarried — but ill, and ill from love for a man who had spurned her. That snub seemed to rebound somehow onto Levin himself. Vronsky had slighted her; she had slighted him, Levin. By that logic Vronsky now had grounds to look down on Levin, which made him an enemy. But Levin didn't think it through that clearly. He vaguely sensed that something in it all was insulting to him, and his irritation now had no particular target — he found fault with everything in front of him. The stupid sale of the forest, the swindle pulled on Oblonsky and concluded under his own roof, infuriated him.
"Well, all finished?" he said, meeting Stepan Arkadyevitch at the top of the stairs. "Ready for supper?"
"I wouldn't say no. The appetite I work up in the country is something else! Wonderful! Why didn't you offer Ryabinin a bite?"
"Oh, the devil with him!"
"Honestly, the way you treat the man!" said Oblonsky. "You didn't even shake his hand. Why wouldn't you shake his hand?"
"Because I don't shake hands with a waiter, and a waiter is a hundred times the better man."
"What a reactionary you are, really! What about the merging of the classes?" said Oblonsky.
"Anyone who wants to merge them is welcome — it makes me sick."
"A regular reactionary, that's what you are."
"Honestly, I've never thought about what I am. I'm Konstantin Levin, and that's all."
"And Konstantin Levin in a thoroughly bad temper," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, smiling.
"Yes, I'm in a bad temper, and do you know why? Because — forgive me — of your idiotic sale...."
Stepan Arkadyevitch made a good-natured grimace, like someone being teased and attacked for no fault of his own.

"Come on, enough of that!" he said. "When has anyone ever sold anything without being told, the moment the deal closes, 'It was worth far more than that'? And yet when you want to sell, nobody will offer you a kopeck.... No, I see you've taken a real dislike to poor old Ryabinin."

"Maybe I have. And do you know why? You'll call me a reactionary again, or some other dreadful name — but it genuinely upsets me and angers me to see, on every side, the impoverishment of the nobility I belong to. And, in spite of the merging of the classes, I'm glad to belong to it. And their impoverishment isn't from extravagance — that would be nothing; living in good style is what's proper for noblemen; only the gentry know how to do it. The peasants around us are buying land, and I don't mind that at all. The gentleman does nothing while the peasant works and pushes the idler aside. That's how it should be. And I'm genuinely glad for the peasant. But what I do mind is watching this process of impoverishment from a kind of — I don't know what to call it — innocence. Here a Polish speculator buys a magnificent estate at half price from a young lady living in Nice. There a merchant gets three acres of land worth ten roubles as security against a loan of one rouble. Here, for no earthly reason, you've handed that scoundrel a gift of thirty thousand roubles."
"Well, what was I supposed to do? Count every tree?"
"Of course they have to be counted. You didn't count them — but Ryabinin did. Ryabinin's children will have a living and an education, while yours, perhaps, will not!"

"Forgive me, but there's something petty about this counting. We have our line of business, they have theirs, and they have to make their profit. Anyway, the thing's done, and that's that. Ah, here come the poached eggs — my favorite dish. And Agafea Mihalovna will give us that marvelous herb-brandy...."
Stepan Arkadyevitch sat down at the table and started joking with Agafea Mihalovna, swearing it had been ages since he'd tasted a dinner or supper like this one.
"Well, at least you praise it," said Agafea Mihalovna, "but as for Konstantin Dmitrievitch, give him whatever you like — a crust of bread — he'll eat it and walk off."

Try as Levin might to control himself, he stayed gloomy and silent. There was one question he wanted to put to Stepan Arkadyevitch, but he couldn't bring himself to it, couldn't find the words or the right moment. Stepan Arkadyevitch had gone downstairs to his room, undressed, washed again, and got into bed in a nightshirt with goffered frills, and Levin still lingered in his room, chattering about trivial things and not daring to ask what he wanted to know.

"It really is wonderful how they make this soap," he said, examining a piece of soap he was turning over in his hands — a piece Agafea Mihalovna had set out for the guest, though Oblonsky hadn't used it. "Just look — it's practically a work of art."

"Yes, everything has been perfected to such a pitch nowadays," said Stepan Arkadyevitch with a damp, contented yawn. "The theater, for example, and the entertainments... a-a-ah!" he yawned. "And electric light everywhere... a-a-ah!"
"Yes, the electric light," said Levin. "Yes. Oh — and where is Vronsky now?" he asked abruptly, setting down the soap.

"Vronsky?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, checking his yawn. "He's in Petersburg. He left soon after you did, and he hasn't been back to Moscow since. And do you know, Kostya, I'll tell you frankly," he went on, leaning his elbow on the table and propping his handsome ruddy face on his hand, the moist, good-natured, sleepy eyes shining like stars. "It's your own fault. You took fright at the sight of your rival. But, as I told you at the time, I couldn't say which of you had the better chance. Why didn't you fight it out? I told you then...." He yawned without opening his mouth.

"Does he know, or doesn't he, that I actually proposed?" Levin wondered, staring at him. "Yes, there's something cagey, something diplomatic in his face," and feeling himself flush, he looked Stepan Arkadyevitch full in the face without a word.

"If there was anything on her side at the time, it was nothing more than a surface attraction," Oblonsky went on. "His being such a perfect aristocrat, you understand, and his future position in society — that had an effect not so much on her as on her mother."
Levin scowled. The humiliation of his rejection stung him to the quick, as if it were a fresh wound only just received. But he was at home, and the walls of one's own home are a kind of support.

"Stop, stop," he began, cutting Oblonsky off. "You go on about his being an aristocrat. But let me ask you — what does it consist of, this aristocracy of Vronsky's or anyone else's, that lets people look down on me? You consider Vronsky an aristocrat; I don't. A man whose father crawled up from nothing by intrigue, and whose mother — God only knows whose mistress she wasn't.... No, excuse me, but I consider myself an aristocrat, and people like me, who can point back in their family history to three or four honorable generations of the highest breeding (talent and intellect, of course, are another matter), and have never curried favor with anyone, never depended on anyone for anything, like my father and my grandfather. I know plenty of such families. You think it small of me to count the trees in my forest, while you make Ryabinin a present of thirty thousand; but you get rents from your estates and God knows what else, while I don't, and so I prize what's come down to me from my ancestors or what I've earned by hard work.... We are the aristocrats, not those who can only exist by the favor of the powerful of this world, and who can be bought for twopence ha'penny."

"Well, but who are you attacking? I agree with you," said Stepan Arkadyevitch sincerely and warmly — though he was perfectly aware that in the category of those who could be bought for twopence ha'penny Levin was counting him too. Levin's heat genuinely pleased him. "Who are you attacking? Though plenty of what you say about Vronsky isn't true, I won't get into that. I'll tell you straight out — if I were you, I'd come back to Moscow with me, and...."

"No; I don't know whether you've heard about it or not, but I don't care. And I'll tell you — I made an offer and was turned down, and Katerina Alexandrovna is nothing to me now but a painful and humiliating memory."
"What on earth for? What nonsense!"

"But let's not talk about it. Please forgive me if I've been disagreeable," said Levin. Now that he had opened up, he was like he had been that morning. "You're not angry with me, Stiva? Please don't be angry," he said, and, smiling, he took his hand.

"Of course not — not in the least, and no reason to be. I'm glad we've spoken openly. And, you know, the early-morning shooting is unusually good — why not come along? I couldn't sleep tonight anyway, so I might go straight from the shoot to the station."
"Excellent."

title: Chapter 18
paragraphs: Although Vronsky's entire inner life was consumed by his passion, his outer life followed, unaltered and inevitable, the familiar grooves of his social and regimental ties and obligations. The interests of his regiment held an important place in Vronsky's life, both because he was fond of the regiment and because the regiment was fond of him. The men in his regiment were not merely fond of Vronsky; they respected him and were proud of him — proud that a man with his enormous wealth, his brilliant education and abilities, with every kind of success, distinction, and ambition open to him, had brushed all that aside, and out of all the interests in life held closest the interests of his regiment and his comrades. Vronsky was aware of his comrades' view of him, and beyond his fondness for the life he felt bound to live up to that reputation.

It goes without saying that he never spoke of his love to any of his comrades, never let the secret slip even in the wildest drinking bouts (though in truth he was never drunk enough to lose control of himself). And he shut up any thoughtless comrade who tried to hint at the affair. But for all that, his love was the talk of the whole town; everyone guessed, with more or less certainty, at his relations with Madame Karenina. Most of the younger men envied him precisely for what was the most galling element of his love — the high standing of Karenin, and the consequent public visibility of their connection in society.

Most of the young women, who envied Anna and had long been tired of hearing her called _virtuous_, were delighted that their predictions were coming true, and were only waiting for a decisive shift in public opinion to fall upon her with the full weight of their scorn. They were already preparing their handfuls of mud to fling when the moment was right. Most of the middle-aged people and certain great personages were displeased by the prospect of the impending scandal in society.

Vronsky's mother, when she first heard of the affair, was pleased — nothing, to her mind, put a finer finishing touch on a brilliant young man than a _liaison_ in the highest society. She was also pleased that Madame Karenina, who had taken her fancy and had spoken so much about her son, was, after all, just like any other pretty, well-bred woman — at least according to Countess Vronskaya's notions. But she had heard lately that her son had turned down a position of great importance to his career simply in order to stay on in the regiment, where he could see Madame Karenina constantly. She learned that great personages were displeased with him on that account, and she changed her opinion. She was also vexed because, from everything she could gather about this attachment, it wasn't the brilliant, graceful, worldly _liaison_ she would have welcomed, but a sort of Wertherish, desperate passion — so she was told — which might well lead him into something rash. She had not seen him since his abrupt departure from Moscow, and she sent her elder son to summon him for a visit.

This elder son was also displeased with his younger brother. He did not distinguish what kind of love this might be — great or small, passionate or detached, lasting or fleeting (he kept a ballet girl himself, although he was a family man, so in such matters he was lenient) — but he knew that this affair was viewed unfavorably by the very people who needed to be pleased, and so he disapproved of his brother's conduct.
Besides the service and society, Vronsky had another great interest — horses; he was passionately fond of horses.

That year an officers' races meet, with a steeplechase, had been organized. Vronsky had entered his name, bought a thoroughbred English mare, and, in spite of his love affair, was looking forward to the races with intense though carefully concealed excitement....
These two passions did not get in each other's way. On the contrary, he needed an occupation and a distraction separate from his love, to recover and rest from the violent emotions tearing at him.

title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: On the day of the races at Krasnoe Selo, Vronsky had come earlier than usual to eat his beefsteak in the regiment's common messroom. He had no need to be strict with himself — he had been brought down to the required light weight very quickly — but he still had to avoid putting on flesh, so he stayed off starchy and sweet dishes. He sat with his coat unbuttoned over a white waistcoat, both elbows on the table, and while he waited for the steak he had ordered, he stared down at a French novel lying open on his plate. He was only looking at the book to avoid conversation with the officers coming and going; he was thinking.

He was thinking of Anna's promise to see him that day after the races. But he hadn't seen her for three days, and as her husband had just returned from abroad, he did not know whether she would be able to meet him today, and he had no idea how to find out. He had had his last meeting with her at his cousin Betsy's summer villa. He visited the Karenins' summer villa as seldom as possible. Now he wanted to go there, and he turned over in his mind how to manage it.

"Of course I'll say Betsy sent me to ask whether she's coming to the races. Of course, I'll go," he decided, lifting his head from the book. And as he pictured vividly the joy of seeing her, his face lit up.

"Send to the house and tell them to harness the carriage and three horses as quickly as they can," he told the servant who was setting down the steak on a hot silver dish, and pulling the dish toward him, he began to eat.

From the billiard room next door came the click of balls, voices, laughter. Two officers appeared at the doorway: one a young fellow with a delicate, sickly face, lately come into the regiment from the Corps of Pages; the other a plump, elderly officer with a bracelet on his wrist and tiny eyes lost in folds of fat.
Vronsky glanced at them, frowned, and looking down at his book as if he hadn't seen them, kept on eating and reading at the same time.
"What — fortifying yourself for your work?" said the plump officer, sitting down beside him.
"As you see," Vronsky replied, frowning, wiping his mouth, and not looking at the officer.
"So you're not afraid of putting on weight?" the man went on, turning a chair around for the young officer.
"What?" Vronsky snapped, with a grimace of disgust that showed his even teeth.
"You're not afraid of getting fat?"
"Waiter — sherry!" Vronsky said without answering, and, moving the book to the other side of him, went on reading.
The plump officer took up the wine list and turned to the young officer.
"You choose what we're drinking," he said, handing him the card and looking at him.

"Rhine wine, please," said the young officer, stealing a timid glance at Vronsky and pulling at the wisp of mustache that was barely visible on his lip. When he saw that Vronsky did not look around, the young officer stood up.
"Let's go into the billiard room," he said.
The plump officer rose obediently, and the two of them moved toward the door.
At that moment, the tall, well-built figure of Captain Yashvin came striding into the room. With a nod of lofty contempt aimed at the two officers, he made straight for Vronsky.
"Ah — here he is!" he cried, bringing his big hand down hard on Vronsky's epaulet. Vronsky looked round angrily, but his face brightened at once with that characteristic look of genial, manly calm.
"That's it, Alexey," said the captain in his loud baritone. "All you can do now is eat a mouthful and have one small glass."
"Oh, I'm not hungry."

"There go the inseparables," Yashvin remarked, glancing mockingly at the two officers just leaving the room. He bent his long legs, sheathed in tight riding breeches, and lowered himself into the chair, which was too low for him, so that his knees jutted up at a sharp angle.
"Why didn't you turn up at the Red Theater last night? Numerova wasn't bad at all. Where were you?"
"I stayed late at the Tverskoys'," said Vronsky.
"Ah!" Yashvin responded.

Yashvin — a gambler, a rake, a man not merely without moral principles but of openly immoral ones — was Vronsky's closest friend in the regiment. Vronsky liked him for his exceptional physical strength, which Yashvin demonstrated mostly by being able to drink like a fish and go without sleep with no visible effect; and also for his great strength of character, which showed in his dealings with both comrades and superiors, commanding fear and respect alike; and at cards, where he played for tens of thousands and, however much he might have drunk, did so with such skill and decisiveness that he was reckoned the best player in the English Club. Vronsky respected and liked Yashvin especially because he felt that Yashvin liked him — not for his name and his money, but for himself. And of all men, he was the only one to whom Vronsky would have liked to talk about his love. He had a feeling that Yashvin, despite his apparent scorn for every kind of feeling, was the only man who could, as Vronsky imagined it, understand the immense passion that now filled his entire life. Moreover, he was sure Yashvin took no pleasure in gossip and scandal, and read his feeling correctly — that is, knew and believed that this passion was no joke, no diversion, but something more serious and important.
Vronsky had never spoken to him about his passion, but he was aware that he knew all about it, and put the right reading on it, and it pleased him to see that in his eyes.
"Ah, yes," Yashvin said when he heard that Vronsky had been at the Tverskoys'; and his black eyes shining, he tugged at his left mustache and started twisting it into his mouth — a bad habit of his.
"Well, and what about you yesterday? Win anything?" Vronsky asked.
"Eight thousand. But three of it doesn't count; he won't pay up."
"Then you can afford to lose on me," said Vronsky, laughing. (Yashvin had wagered heavily on Vronsky in the races.)
"No chance I'll lose. Mahotin's the only one to worry about."
And the conversation drifted to predictions about the coming race — the only thing Vronsky could think about just then.
"Come on, I'm done," said Vronsky, and, getting up, he went to the door. Yashvin rose too, stretching his long legs and long back.
"It's too early for me to dine, but I do need a drink. I'll catch up with you in a minute. Hi — wine!" he shouted in the rich voice that always boomed out at drill, now rattling the windows.
"No, never mind," he shouted again right after. "You're going home, so I'll come with you."
And he walked out with Vronsky.

title: Chapter 20
paragraphs: Vronsky was staying in a roomy, clean, Finnish hut, divided in two by a partition. Petritsky was billeted with him in camp. Petritsky was still asleep when Vronsky and Yashvin came in.
"Get up — stop sleeping," said Yashvin, going behind the partition and giving Petritsky, who lay with hair tousled and his nose in the pillow, a prod on the shoulder.
Petritsky jumped abruptly to his knees and looked around.

"Your brother was here," he said to Vronsky. "He woke me up, damn him, and said he'd come back." He pulled the rug up and flung himself back on the pillow. "Oh, shut up, Yashvin!" he said, furious at Yashvin for tugging the rug off him. "Shut up!" He rolled over and opened his eyes. "You'd better tell me what to drink — the taste in my mouth is foul, it's...."
"Brandy is better than anything," Yashvin boomed. "Tereshtchenko — brandy for your master, and cucumbers!" he shouted, obviously enjoying the sound of his own voice.

"Brandy, you think? Eh?" Petritsky asked, blinking and rubbing his eyes. "And you'll have one too? All right then, we'll drink together! Vronsky, will you have a drink?" said Petritsky, getting up and wrapping the tiger-skin rug around himself. He went to the doorway in the partition wall, raised his hands and hummed in French, "There was a king in Thule." "Vronsky, will you have a drink?"
"Get going," said Vronsky, putting on the coat his valet handed him.
"Where are you off to?" asked Yashvin. "Oh, here are your three horses," he added, seeing the carriage drive up.
"To the stables — and I have to see Bryansky too, about the horses," said Vronsky.

Vronsky had in fact promised to call at Bryansky's, about eight miles from Peterhof, to bring him some money owed on some horses, and he was hoping to fit that in as well. But his comrades realized at once that he was not going only there.
Petritsky, still humming, winked and pursed his lips, as if to say: "Oh yes, we know your Bryansky."

"Mind you're not late!" was Yashvin's only comment; and to change the subject: "How's my roan? Holding up?" he asked, peering out of the window at the middle horse of the three, the one he had sold Vronsky.
"Wait!" Petritsky called after Vronsky as he was on his way out. "Your brother left a letter and a note for you. Hold on — where are they?"
Vronsky stopped.
"Well — where are they?"
"Where are they? That's the question!" Petritsky said solemnly, moving his forefinger up from his nose.
"Come on, out with it — this is silly," said Vronsky, smiling.
"I haven't lit the fire. They're around here somewhere."
"Enough fooling. Where is the letter?"

"No, I've honestly forgotten. Or was it a dream? Hold on — hold on! What's the use of getting angry? If you'd drunk four bottles yesterday the way I did, you'd forget where you were lying. Wait a moment, I'll remember!"
Petritsky went behind the partition and lay down on his bed.
"Wait! Here's how I was lying, and here's how he was standing. Yes — yes — yes.... Here it is!" — and Petritsky pulled a letter out from under the mattress where he had hidden it.

Vronsky took the letter and his brother's note. It was the letter he had been expecting — from his mother, scolding him for not having been to see her — and the note was from his brother saying he needed a short talk with him. Vronsky knew it was all about the same thing. "What business is it of theirs!" he thought, and, crumpling the letters, he stuffed them between the buttons of his coat to read carefully on the way. In the porch of the hut he was met by two officers; one from his regiment and one from another.
Vronsky's quarters were always a gathering place for all the officers.
"Where are you off to?"
"I have to go to Peterhof."
"Has the mare arrived from Tsarskoe?"
"Yes, but I haven't seen her yet."
"They say Mahotin's Gladiator's gone lame."
"Nonsense! But how on earth will you race in this mud?" said the other.
"Here come my saviors!" cried Petritsky, seeing them enter. The orderly stood in front of him with a tray of brandy and salted cucumbers. "Yashvin here is ordering me to drink a pick-me-up."
"Well, you really put us through it yesterday," said one of the new arrivals. "You didn't let us sleep a wink all night."

"Oh, didn't we wrap it up nicely!" said Petritsky. "Volkov climbed onto the roof and started telling us how sad he was. I said: 'Let's have music — the funeral march!' He fell flat asleep on the roof to the funeral march."

"Drink it up; you absolutely have to drink the brandy, and then seltzer water and plenty of lemon," said Yashvin, standing over Petritsky like a mother making a child take medicine, "and then a little champagne — just a small bottle."
"Now that makes sense. Hold on a moment, Vronsky. We'll all have a drink."
"No — goodbye, all of you. I'm not drinking today."
"Why — putting on weight? All right, then we'll have to do it without you. Give us the seltzer water and lemon."
"Vronsky!" someone shouted when he was already outside.
"Yes?"
"You'd better get a haircut — it'll weigh you down, especially on top."
Vronsky was in fact starting prematurely to thin a little on top. He laughed gaily, showing his even teeth, and, pulling his cap down over the thin spot, went out and climbed into his carriage.

"To the stables!" he said, and was just pulling out the letters to read through, when he thought better of it and decided to put off reading them so as not to distract himself before looking at the mare. "Later!"

title: Chapter 21
paragraphs: The temporary stable, a wooden shed, had been put up near the racecourse, and his mare was supposed to have been moved there the day before. He hadn't yet been to see her.

Over the last few days he hadn't ridden her out for exercise himself, but had left her in the trainer's hands, so right now he really had no idea what condition his mare had arrived in yesterday and was in today. He had barely stepped out of his carriage when his groom, the so-called "stable boy," recognizing the carriage from a distance, called for the trainer. A lean Englishman in tall boots and a short jacket, clean-shaven except for a tuft below his chin, came to meet him, walking with the awkward gait of a jockey, elbows turned outward and his body rocking from side to side.
"Well, how's Frou-Frou?" Vronsky asked in English.

"All right, sir," the Englishman's voice answered, somewhere down in his throat. "Better not go in," he added, touching his hat. "I've put a muzzle on her, and the mare's jumpy. Better not go in — it'll set her off."
"No, I'm going in. I want a look at her."
"Come along then," said the Englishman, frowning, speaking through closed lips, and with swinging elbows he led the way at his uneven gait.

They went into the small yard in front of the shed. A stable boy, smart and spruce in his holiday clothes, met them with a broom in hand and followed them in. In the shed there were five horses in separate stalls, and Vronsky knew that his chief rival, Gladiator, a very tall chestnut, had been brought here and must be standing among them. Even more than his own mare, Vronsky was longing to see Gladiator, whom he had never laid eyes on. But he knew that, by the etiquette of the racecourse, it was not only impossible for him to look at the horse but improper even to ask about him. As he was walking down the corridor, the boy opened the door to the second box on the left, and Vronsky caught a glimpse of a big chestnut horse with white legs. He knew this was Gladiator, but, with the feeling of a man turning his eyes away from another man's open letter, he turned and went into Frou-Frou's stall.
"The horse in here belongs to Mak... Mak... I can never get the name out," said the Englishman over his shoulder, jabbing his big finger with its dirty nail in the direction of Gladiator's stall.
"Mahotin? Yes — he's my most serious rival," said Vronsky.
"If you were riding him," the Englishman said, "I'd bet on you."
"Frou-Frou is more nervous; he is stronger," Vronsky said, smiling at the compliment to his riding.
"In a steeplechase, everything depends on the riding and on pluck," said the Englishman.

Of pluck — meaning energy and courage — Vronsky did not merely feel he had enough; what mattered far more, he was firmly convinced that no one in the world could possess more of this "pluck" than he did.
"You don't think I need to lose more weight?"

"Oh no," the Englishman answered. "Please don't speak loudly. The mare's jumpy," he added, nodding toward the horse-box, before which they were standing, and from which came the sound of restless stamping in the straw.

He opened the door, and Vronsky stepped into the horse-box, dimly lit by one small window. In the box stood a dark bay mare with a muzzle on, pawing at the fresh straw. Looking around him in the twilight of the box, Vronsky unconsciously took in once more, in a single sweeping glance, every point of his favorite mare. Frou-Frou was a beast of medium size, not entirely beyond reproach from a breeder's point of view. She was small-boned all over; though her chest was extremely prominent in front, it was narrow. Her hindquarters drooped a little, and in her forelegs, and still more in her hind legs, there was a noticeable bow. The muscles of both fore- and hind legs were not very heavy; but across her shoulders the mare was exceptionally broad — a feature especially striking now that she was lean from training. The bones of her legs below the knees looked, from the front, no thicker than a finger, but seen from the side they were extraordinarily thick. Apart from across her shoulders, she looked overall as though she had been pinched in at the sides and stretched out in depth. But she had, to the highest degree, the quality that makes one forget every fault: that quality was _blood_, the blood _that tells_, as the English expression puts it. Her muscles stood up sharply under the network of sinews, beneath a delicate, mobile skin soft as satin, and they were hard as bone. Her cleanly cut head, with its prominent, bright, spirited eyes, broadened at the open nostrils, which showed the red blood in the cartilage within. About her whole figure, and especially her head, there was a certain look of energy combined with softness. She was one of those creatures who seem unable to speak only because the structure of their mouths will not allow it.
To Vronsky, at any rate, it seemed that she understood everything he was feeling at that moment as he looked at her.

As soon as Vronsky stepped toward her she drew in a long breath and, rolling back her prominent eye until the white showed bloodshot, she shied at the approaching figures from the opposite side, shaking her muzzle and shifting lightly from one leg to the other.
"There — you see how jumpy she is," said the Englishman.
"There, my darling — there!" said Vronsky, going up to the mare and speaking soothingly to her.

But the closer he came, the more agitated she grew. Only when he was right at her head did she suddenly quiet, with the muscles trembling beneath her soft, delicate coat. Vronsky patted her strong neck, smoothed a stray lock of mane that had fallen on the wrong side of her sharp withers, and brought his face up close to her flared nostrils, sheer as a bat's wing. She drew a loud breath, snorted out through her tense nostrils, started, pricked her sharp ear, and stretched her strong black lip out toward Vronsky as if she wanted to nip his sleeve. Then, remembering the muzzle, she shook it, and once more began stamping restlessly with one shapely leg after another.
"Easy, my darling, easy!" he said, patting her again on the hindquarters; and, with the joyful sense that his mare was in the best possible condition, he stepped out of the box.
The mare's excitement had infected Vronsky. He felt his heart pounding, and he, too, like the mare, wanted to move, to bite; it was both dreadful and delicious.
"Well, I'm counting on you, then," he said to the Englishman; "half-past six on the ground."
"All right," said the Englishman. "Oh — where are you going, my lord?" he asked suddenly, using the title "my lord," which he had scarcely ever used before.

Vronsky raised his head in surprise and stared, in the way he knew how to stare — not into the Englishman's eyes but at his forehead — astonished at the impertinence of the question. But realizing that in asking it the Englishman had been speaking to him not as an employer but as a jockey, he answered:
"I've got to go to Bryansky's; I'll be home within an hour."

"That's the question I've been asked over and over today!" he said to himself, and he blushed — something that rarely happened to him. The Englishman looked gravely at him; and, as though he too knew where Vronsky was going, he added:
"The main thing's to stay calm before a race," he said. "Don't lose your temper, don't get worked up about anything."
"All right," Vronsky answered, smiling; and jumping into his carriage, he told the driver to head for Peterhof.
He had barely driven a few paces before the dark clouds that had been threatening rain all day broke, and a heavy downpour came down.

"What a shame!" thought Vronsky, putting up the roof of the carriage. "It was muddy before — now it'll be a perfect swamp." Alone in the closed carriage, he took out his mother's letter and his brother's note, and read them through.

Yes, it was the same thing all over again. Everyone — his mother, his brother, everyone — felt entitled to meddle in his heart's affairs. Their meddling stirred up in him a feeling of angry hatred — a feeling he had rarely known before. "What business is it of theirs? Why does everyone feel called on to make me his concern? And why do they have to badger me so? Just because they sense this is something they don't understand. If it were a common, vulgar, society intrigue, they would leave me alone. They feel this is something different, that this is not a mere amusement, that this woman is dearer to me than life. And that's incomprehensible to them, and that's why it makes them angry. Whatever our fate is or may be, we have made it ourselves, and we don't complain of it," he said, joining himself with Anna in the word _we_. "No, they have to teach us how to live. They have no idea what happiness is; they don't know that without our love, there is for us neither happiness nor unhappiness — no life at all," he thought.

He was angry with all of them for their meddling precisely because in his soul he felt that they — all these people — were right. He felt that the love that bound him to Anna was no momentary impulse that would pass, as society intrigues do pass, leaving in the life of either nothing more than pleasant or unpleasant memories. He felt all the torture of his own position and hers, all the difficulty of concealing their love when they were so conspicuous in the eyes of the world, of lying and deceiving — and of lying, deceiving, pretending, constantly thinking about other people, when the passion that bound them was so intense that they were both oblivious to anything but their love.

He pictured vividly all the constantly recurring instances when lying and deceit were forced on him — things so against his natural bent. He recalled particularly vividly the shame he had more than once seen in her at the necessity of such lying. And he had that strange feeling that had come over him several times since his secret love for Anna began. It was a feeling of loathing for something — whether for Alexey Alexandrovitch, or for himself, or for the world as a whole, he could not have said. But he always drove this strange feeling away. He shook it off now too, and picked up the thread of his thoughts.
"Yes — she was unhappy before, but proud and at peace; and now she cannot be at peace and feel secure in her dignity, though she does not show it. Yes, we have to put an end to this," he decided.

And for the first time the thought clearly took shape in him that it was essential to put an end to this false position, and the sooner the better. "Throw everything off, she and I, and hide ourselves somewhere alone with our love," he said to himself.

title: Chapter 22
paragraphs: The rain didn't last long, and by the time Vronsky arrived — his shaft horse trotting at full speed, dragging the trace horses at a gallop through the mud, their reins hanging loose — the sun had peeked out again, and the roofs of the summer villas and the old lime trees in the gardens along both sides of the main street sparkled with wet brilliance, and from the twigs came a pleasant drip and from the roofs water poured in rushing streams. He no longer thought about the rain ruining the racecourse; he was glad now that — thanks to the rain — he was sure to find her at home and alone, since he knew that Alexey Alexandrovitch, just back from a foreign watering place, had not budged from Petersburg.

Hoping to find her alone, Vronsky got out, as he always did, before crossing the bridge, to avoid attracting attention, and walked the rest of the way to the house. He did not go up the steps to the front door, but went round to the courtyard.
"Has your master come?" he asked a gardener.
"No, sir. The mistress is at home. But please go to the front door — there are servants there," the gardener answered. "They'll open it for you."
"No, I'll go in from the garden."

Satisfied that she was alone, and wanting to surprise her — since he hadn't promised to come today, and she would surely not expect him before the races — he walked, holding his sword and stepping carefully along the sandy path bordered with flowers, toward the terrace looking out over the garden. Vronsky forgot now everything he had been thinking on the way about the hardships and difficulties of their position. He thought only of how he was about to see her, not in his imagination, but living, all of her, as she really was. He was just going in, planting his foot flat on each tread so as not to make the worn steps of the terrace creak, when he suddenly remembered what he always forgot, and what made the most painful side of his relations with her — her son with his questioning eyes, hostile, as Vronsky imagined them.

This boy was, more than anyone else, a check on their freedom. When he was around, both Vronsky and Anna not only avoided talking about anything they couldn't have said in front of everyone — they didn't even allow themselves to refer by hints to anything the boy didn't understand. They had made no agreement about this; it had settled itself. They would have felt it shameful to lie to the child. In his presence they spoke like acquaintances. But in spite of this caution, Vronsky often caught the child's intent, bewildered glance fixed on him, and noticed a strange shyness, uncertainty — sometimes friendliness, sometimes coldness and reserve — in the boy's manner toward him, as if the child sensed that between this man and his mother there was some important bond whose meaning he could not grasp.

In fact the boy did feel that he couldn't understand this connection, and he tried painfully, and could not manage, to work out what he was supposed to feel for this man. With a child's keen instinct for every shade of feeling, he saw clearly that his father, his governess, his nurse — all of them not only disliked Vronsky but looked on him with horror and revulsion, though they never said a word about him — while his mother regarded him as her greatest friend.

"What does it mean? Who is he? How am I supposed to love him? If I don't know, it's my fault — either I'm stupid or a bad boy," thought the child. And that was what produced the doubtful, questioning, sometimes hostile expression, and the shyness and uncertainty that Vronsky found so unbearable. This child's presence always and infallibly stirred up in Vronsky that strange feeling of inexplicable loathing he had been having lately. The child's presence aroused in both Vronsky and Anna a feeling like that of a sailor who sees by the compass that the direction in which he is moving rapidly is far from the right one, but knows it isn't in his power to stop, that every instant is carrying him further off, and that to admit to himself his deviation from the right course is the same as admitting his certain ruin.
This child, with his innocent view of the world, was the compass that showed them how far they had strayed from what they knew but did not want to know.

This time Seryozha was not at home, and she was completely alone. She was sitting on the terrace waiting for the return of her son, who had gone out for a walk and been caught in the rain. She had sent a manservant and a maid out to look for him. Wearing a white gown with deep embroidery, she was sitting in a corner of the terrace behind some flowers, and didn't hear him. With her curly black head bent, she pressed her forehead against a cool watering pot that stood on the parapet, and both of her lovely hands, with the rings he knew so well, clasped the pot. The beauty of her whole figure, her head, her neck, her hands, struck Vronsky each time as something new and unexpected. He stood still, gazing at her in ecstasy. But the moment he took a step toward her, she sensed his presence, pushed the watering pot away, and turned her flushed face to him.

"What's the matter? Are you ill?" he said to her in French, going up to her. He would have run to her, but, remembering that there might be people watching, he glanced toward the balcony door and flushed a little, as he always did when feeling that he had to be afraid and on his guard.
"No, I'm quite well," she said, getting up and pressing his outstretched hand tightly. "I didn't expect... thee."
"Mercy — what cold hands!" he said.
"You startled me," she said. "I'm alone, waiting for Seryozha; he's out for a walk; they'll be coming in from this side."
But for all her efforts to be calm, her lips were trembling.

"Forgive me for coming, but I couldn't get through the day without seeing you," he went on, speaking French, as he always did, to avoid the stiff Russian plural form, so impossibly cold between them, and the dangerously intimate singular.
"Forgive you? I'm so glad you're here!"
"But you're ill or troubled," he went on, still holding her hands and bending over her. "What were you thinking about?"
"Always the same thing," she said with a smile.

She was telling the truth. If at any moment she had been asked what she was thinking about, she could have answered honestly: of the same thing — of her happiness and her unhappiness. She was thinking, just as he came upon her, of this: why, she wondered, was it that for others, for Betsy (she knew about her secret affair with Tushkevitch), it was all easy, while for her it was such torture? Today this thought had taken on particular sharpness from certain other things. She asked him about the races. He answered her questions, and, seeing that she was agitated, trying to calm her, he began to tell her in the most matter-of-fact tone the details of his preparations for the races.

"Tell him or not tell him?" she thought, looking into his quiet, affectionate eyes. "He is so happy, so absorbed in his races, that he won't understand the way he ought, he won't understand all the weight of this fact for us."
"But you haven't told me what you were thinking about when I came in," he said, breaking off his story. "Please tell me!"

She didn't answer, and, bowing her head a little, she looked at him questioningly from under her brows, her eyes shining beneath their long lashes. Her hand shook as it played with a leaf she had picked. He saw it, and his face took on that look of utter surrender, of slavish devotion, that had done so much to win her.
"I can see something has happened. Do you suppose I can be at peace knowing you have a trouble I'm not sharing? Tell me, for God's sake," he repeated imploringly.

"Yes, I won't be able to forgive him if he doesn't realize all the seriousness of it. Better not tell — why put him to the test?" she thought, still staring at him in the same way, and feeling the hand holding the leaf was trembling more and more.
"For God's sake!" he repeated, taking her hand.
"Shall I tell you?"
"Yes, yes, yes...."

"I am with child," she said, softly and deliberately. The leaf in her hand shook more violently, but she did not take her eyes off him, watching to see how he would take it. He went pale, was about to say something, and stopped; he dropped her hand, and his head sank on his chest. "Yes, he realizes all the gravity of it," she thought, and she pressed his hand gratefully.

But she was wrong to think he realized the gravity of the fact as she, a woman, realized it. On hearing it, he felt that strange feeling of loathing for someone come over him with ten times the force. But at the same time he felt that the turning point he had been longing for had now arrived; that it was no longer possible to keep things from her husband, and that, one way or another, they would soon have to put an end to their unnatural position. Beyond that, her emotion physically affected him in the same way it had affected her. He looked at her with a look of submissive tenderness, kissed her hand, got up, and silently paced up and down the terrace.

"Yes," he said, going up to her firmly. "Neither you nor I have looked on our relations as a passing amusement, and now our fate is decided. We absolutely must put an end" — he glanced around as he spoke — "to the deception we are living in."
"Put an end? How put an end, Alexey?" she said softly.
She was calmer now, and her face lit up with a tender smile.
"Leave your husband and let us make our life one."
"It is one as it is," she answered, barely audibly.
"Yes — but altogether; altogether."
"But how, Alexey, tell me how?" she said in melancholy mockery at the hopelessness of her own position. "Is there any way out of such a position? Am I not my husband's wife?"

"There is a way out of every position. We have to take our course," he said. "Anything is better than the position you're living in. Of course I see how you torture yourself over everything — the world, your son, your husband."
"Oh, not over my husband," she said with a quiet smile. "I don't know him, I don't think of him. He doesn't exist."
"You're not being honest. I know you. You worry about him too."

"Oh, he doesn't even know," she said, and suddenly a hot flush spread across her face; her cheeks, her brow, her neck went crimson, and tears of shame came into her eyes. "But we won't talk about him."

title: Chapter 23
paragraphs: Vronsky had several times before, though not as firmly as now, tried to bring her to consider their position, and every time he had been met by the same superficial, dismissive tone with which she met his appeal now. It was as if there were something in this that she could not or would not face — as if the moment she began to talk about it, she, the real Anna, somehow withdrew into herself, and another, strange, unaccountable woman emerged, whom he did not love, whom he feared, and who set herself against him. But today he was determined to have it out.
"Whether he knows or doesn't," said Vronsky in his usual quiet, resolute tone, "that's nothing to do with us. We cannot... you cannot stay like this, especially now."

"And what should be done, in your view?" she asked with the same frivolous irony. She, who had been so afraid he would take her condition too lightly, was now annoyed with him for drawing from it the conclusion that they had to take some step.
"Tell him everything, and leave him."

"Very well, let's say I do that," she said. "Do you know what the result would be? I can tell you in advance," and a vicious light gleamed in her eyes, which had been so soft only a moment before. "'Eh, you love another man, and have entered into a criminal liaison with him?'" (Mimicking her husband, she stressed the word "criminal," as Alexey Alexandrovitch did.) "'I warned you of the consequences in the religious, the civil, and the domestic sphere. You did not listen to me. Now I cannot allow you to disgrace my name — '" "and my son," she had meant to say, but about her son she could not joke, "' — disgrace my name, and' — and more in the same vein," she added. "In short, he'll say in his official manner, with all clarity and precision, that he cannot let me go, but will take every measure in his power to prevent scandal. And he will calmly and methodically carry out his words. That's what will happen. He is not a man — he is a machine, and a vindictive machine when he's angry," she added, picturing Alexey Alexandrovitch as she spoke, with all the peculiarities of his figure and his manner of speaking, and counting against him every fault she could find in him, sparing him nothing for the great wrong she was doing him.
"But, Anna," said Vronsky in a soft, persuasive voice, trying to calm her, "we absolutely must tell him, no matter what, and then be guided by whatever line he takes."
"What — run away?"
"And why not run away? I don't see how we can go on like this. And not for my sake — I can see how you suffer."
"Yes — run away and become your mistress," she said angrily.
"Anna," he said with reproachful tenderness.
"Yes," she went on, "become your mistress, and complete the ruin of...."
Again she would have said "my son," but she could not speak the word.

Vronsky could not understand how she, with her strong, truthful nature, could go on enduring this state of deceit, and not long to get out of it. But he did not suspect that the chief cause of it was that one word — _son_ — which she could not bring herself to say. When she thought of her son, and of his future attitude toward his mother, who had left his father, she felt such terror at what she had done that she could not face it; but, like a woman, she could only try to comfort herself with lying assurances that everything would stay as it had always been, and that she could somehow forget the dreadful question of what would become of her son.
"I beg you, I implore you," she said suddenly, taking his hand, speaking in a quite different tone, sincere and tender, "never speak to me of that!"
"But, Anna...."

"Never. Leave it to me. I know all the baseness, all the horror of my position — but it isn't as easy to arrange as you think. Leave it to me, and do as I say. Never speak to me about it. Do you promise?... No, no, promise!..."
"I promise everything, but I can't be at peace — especially after what you've told me. I can't be at peace when you can't be...."
"I?" she repeated. "Yes, I worry sometimes; but it will pass, if you never talk about this. When you talk about it — that's the only time it troubles me."
"I don't understand," he said.
"I know," she interrupted him, "how hard it is for your truthful nature to lie, and I grieve for you. I often think you've ruined your whole life for me."
"I was just thinking the same thing," he said; "how could you have sacrificed everything for my sake? I can't forgive myself that you're unhappy!"

"I unhappy?" she said, coming closer to him, and looking at him with an ecstatic smile of love. "I am like a hungry man who has been given food. He may be cold, and dressed in rags, and ashamed, but he is not unhappy. I unhappy? No — _this_ is my unhappiness...."

She could hear the sound of her son's voice coming toward them, and, glancing quickly around the terrace, she got up impulsively. Her eyes glowed with the fire he knew so well; with a swift movement she raised her lovely hands, covered with rings, took his head, gave him one long look, and, lifting her face with smiling, parted lips, kissed his mouth and both eyes in quick succession, and pushed him away. She would have gone, but he held her back.
"When?" he murmured in a whisper, gazing at her in ecstasy.
"Tonight, at one o'clock," she whispered, and, with a heavy sigh, she walked with her light, swift step to meet her son.
Seryozha had been caught by the rain in the big garden, and he and his nurse had taken shelter in an arbor.
"Well, _au revoir_," she said to Vronsky. "I have to start getting ready for the races. Betsy promised to fetch me."
Vronsky, glancing at his watch, hurried away.

title: Chapter 24
paragraphs: When Vronsky looked at his watch on the Karenins' balcony, he was so agitated and so lost in his thoughts that he saw the numbers on the dial but couldn't take in what time it was. He went out onto the highroad and walked, picking his way carefully through the mud, to his carriage. He was so completely absorbed in his feeling for Anna that he didn't even consider what time it was, or whether he had time to go to Bryansky's. He was left, as often happens, with only the outer faculty of memory that prompts each next step to be taken. He went up to his coachman, who was dozing on the box in the lengthening shade of a thick lime tree; he stared with mild admiration at the shifting clouds of midges spinning over the hot horses, and, waking the coachman, jumped into the carriage and told him to drive to Bryansky's. It was only after driving nearly five miles that he had recovered enough to look at his watch and realize it was half-past five and he was late.

Several races were scheduled for that day: the Mounted Guards' race, then the officers' mile-and-a-half race, then the three-mile race, and then the race he himself was entered in. He could still make his own race, but if he stopped at Bryansky's he would only just be in time, and would arrive when the entire court was already in its places. That would be a pity. But he had promised Bryansky he would come, and so he decided to push on, telling the coachman not to spare the horses.

He reached Bryansky's, spent five minutes there, and galloped back. This fast drive calmed him. All that was painful in his relations with Anna, all the vagueness left by their conversation, slipped from his mind. He was now thinking with pleasure and excitement of the race, of being on time anyway; and from time to time the thought of the blissful meeting awaiting him that night flashed across his imagination like a leaping flame.

The excitement of the approaching race took hold of him as he drove deeper and deeper into the atmosphere of the racecourse, overtaking carriages coming up from the summer villas or out of Petersburg.

At his quarters no one was home; everyone was at the races, and only his valet was watching for him at the gate. While he changed his clothes, his valet told him that the second race had already started, that several gentlemen had been by asking for him, and that a boy had come up twice from the stables. Dressing without haste (he never hurried, and never lost his composure), Vronsky drove to the sheds. From the sheds he could see a sea of carriages, and people on foot, soldiers ringing the racecourse, and pavilions packed with people. The second race was apparently in progress, because just as he came into the sheds he heard a bell ring. As he walked toward the stable, he passed the white-legged chestnut, Mahotin's Gladiator, being led to the racecourse in a blue forage horsecloth with what looked like huge ears edged in blue.
"Where's Cord?" he asked the stable boy.
"In the stable, putting on the saddle."
In the open box stood Frou-Frou, saddled and ready. They were just about to lead her out.
"I'm not too late?"
"All right! All right!" said the Englishman. "Don't get yourself worked up!"

Vronsky took in once more, in a single glance, the exquisite lines of his favorite mare; she was quivering all over, and with an effort he tore himself from the sight of her and went out of the stable. He walked toward the pavilions at the most favorable moment for slipping past unnoticed. The mile-and-a-half race was just finishing, and every eye was fixed on the horse guard at the front and the light hussar behind, urging their horses on with one last effort close to the winning post. From both the center and the outside of the ring, everyone was crowding toward the post, and a group of soldiers and officers of the horse guards were shouting loudly in delight at the expected triumph of their officer and comrade. Vronsky moved into the middle of the crowd unnoticed, just as the bell rang at the finish of the race, and the tall, mud-splattered horse guard who came in first leaned over the saddle and let go of the reins of his panting gray horse, dark with sweat.

The horse, bracing its legs, with an effort halted its rapid course, and the officer of the horse guards looked round him like a man waking from a heavy sleep, and just managed a smile. A crowd of friends and outsiders pressed round him.

Vronsky deliberately avoided that select crowd of the upper set, which was moving and talking with discreet ease in front of the pavilions. He knew that Madame Karenina was there, and Betsy, and his brother's wife, and he stayed away on purpose for fear something would distract him. But he was constantly stopped by acquaintances who told him about the previous races and kept asking why he was so late.

Just as the racers had to go to the pavilion to receive their prizes, with all attention on that point, Vronsky's elder brother Alexander, a colonel in heavy fringed epaulets, came up to him. He wasn't tall, though as broadly built as Alexey, handsomer than he and rosier; he had a red nose and an open, drunken-looking face.
"Did you get my note?" he said. "It's impossible to track you down."
Alexander Vronsky, despite the dissolute life — and especially the drinking habits for which he was notorious — was very much one of the court circle.

Now, as he spoke to his brother about a matter that was bound to be extremely unwelcome, knowing many eyes might be on him, he kept a smiling expression, as though he were joking with his brother about something trivial.
"I got it, and I really can't make out what _you_ are getting yourself worked up about," said Alexey.
"I'm getting myself worked up because it was just pointed out to me that you weren't here, and that you were seen at Peterhof on Monday."
"There are matters that concern only those directly involved, and the matter you're so worked up about is...."
"Yes — but if so, you might as well leave the service...."
"I'll ask you not to meddle, and that's all I have to say."

Alexey Vronsky's frowning face went white, and his prominent lower jaw quivered — something that rarely happened to him. A man of a very warm heart, he was seldom angry; but when he was, and when his chin shook, then, as Alexander Vronsky knew, he was dangerous. Alexander Vronsky smiled cheerfully.

"I only wanted to give you Mother's letter. Answer it, and don't worry about anything just before the race. _Bonne chance,_" he added, smiling, and stepped away from him. But right after him another friendly greeting pulled Vronsky up short.

"So you won't recognize your friends! How are you, _mon cher?_" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, as conspicuously brilliant in the midst of all the Petersburg brilliance as he was in Moscow, his face rosy, his whiskers sleek and glossy. "I came up yesterday, and I'm delighted I'll get to see your triumph. When shall we meet?"

"Come to the messroom tomorrow," Vronsky said, and, squeezing him by the sleeve of his coat with a quick apology, he made his way to the center of the racecourse, where the horses were being led out for the great steeplechase.

The horses who had run in the last race were being led off, steaming and exhausted, by the stable boys, and one after another the fresh horses for the next race appeared, mostly English racers, in horsecloths, looking — with their tucked-up bellies — like strange, enormous birds. On the right Frou-Frou was led in, lean and beautiful, lifting her elastic, rather long pasterns as though moved by springs. Not far from her they were taking the rug off the lop-eared Gladiator. The strong, exquisite, perfectly correct lines of the stallion, with his superb hindquarters and unusually short pasterns almost on top of his hoofs, caught Vronsky's attention in spite of himself. He would have gone up to his mare, but he was held up again by an acquaintance.
"Oh — there's Karenin!" said the acquaintance he was chatting with. "He's looking for his wife, and she's right in the middle of the pavilion. Did you see her?"
"No," Vronsky answered, and, without even glancing toward the pavilion where his friend was pointing out Madame Karenina, he went up to his mare.

Vronsky had not had time to look at the saddle, about which he needed to give an instruction, when the competitors were called to the pavilion to receive their numbers and positions at the start. Seventeen officers, looking serious and grim, many with pale faces, gathered in the pavilion and drew their numbers. Vronsky drew number seven. The cry rang out: "Mount!"

Feeling that, along with the other riders, he was the center on which every eye was fastened, Vronsky walked up to his mare in that state of nervous tension in which his movements always turned slow and deliberate. Cord, in honor of the races, had put on his best clothes — a black coat buttoned to the top, a stiffly starched collar that propped up his cheeks, a round black hat, and top boots. He was as calm and dignified as ever, and was holding Frou-Frou by both reins himself, standing squarely in front of her. Frou-Frou was still trembling as though in a fever. Her eye, full of fire, glanced sideways at Vronsky. Vronsky slipped his finger under the saddle girth. The mare squinted sideways at him, drew up her lip, and twitched her ear. The Englishman pursed his lips, intending to suggest a smile that anyone should bother to check his saddling.
"Get up — you won't feel so worked up."

Vronsky looked round for the last time at his rivals. He knew he would not see them during the race. Two were already riding ahead to the point from which they would start. Galtsin, a friend of Vronsky's and one of his more serious rivals, was circling a bay horse that would not let him mount. A small, light hussar in tight breeches galloped off, crouched on the saddle like a cat in imitation of English jockeys. Prince Kuzovlev sat with a white face on his thoroughbred mare from the Grabovsky stud, while an English groom led her by the bridle. Vronsky and all his comrades knew Kuzovlev and his peculiar combination of "weak nerves" and terrible vanity. They knew he was afraid of everything, afraid of riding a spirited horse. But now, precisely because it was dangerous, because people broke their necks and there was a doctor stationed at every obstacle, and an ambulance with a cross on it, and a sister of mercy, he had made up his mind to take part. Their eyes met, and Vronsky gave him a friendly, encouraging nod. The only one he did not see was his chief rival, Mahotin on Gladiator.
"Don't be in a hurry," Cord said to Vronsky, "and remember one thing: don't hold her back at the fences, and don't urge her on; let her go as she likes."
"All right, all right," Vronsky said, taking the reins.
"If you can, lead the race; but don't lose heart till the last moment, even if you're behind."

Before the mare had had time to move, Vronsky put his foot, with one agile, vigorous motion, into the steel-toothed stirrup and lightly, firmly settled into the creaking leather of the saddle. Getting his right foot into the stirrup, he smoothed the double reins between his fingers as he always did, and Cord let go.

As though she didn't know which foot to put first, Frou-Frou started off, dragging at the reins with her long neck, and as though on springs, jolting her rider from side to side. Cord quickened his pace to keep up. The excited mare, trying to throw off her rider first on one side, then on the other, pulled at the reins, and Vronsky tried in vain, with voice and hand, to soothe her.

They were just nearing the dammed-up stream on the way to the starting point. Several of the riders were ahead and several behind, when suddenly Vronsky heard the sound of a horse galloping through the mud behind him, and Mahotin overtook him on his white-legged, lop-eared Gladiator. Mahotin smiled, baring his long teeth, but Vronsky shot him an angry look. He didn't like him, and now considered him his most serious rival. He was angry with him for galloping past and stirring up his mare. Frou-Frou started into a gallop, her left foot forward, made two bounds, and, fretting at the tightened reins, dropped into a jolting trot that bumped her rider up and down. Cord, too, frowned, and followed Vronsky almost at a trot.

title: Chapter 25
paragraphs: Seventeen officers in all were riding in this race. The course was a large three-mile elliptical ring in front of the pavilion. Nine obstacles had been laid out on it: the stream; a big, solid barrier five feet high just in front of the pavilion; a dry ditch; a ditch full of water; a steep slope; an Irish barricade (one of the hardest obstacles, consisting of a mound fenced with brushwood, beyond which was a ditch hidden from the horses, so that the horse had to clear both at once or risk a fatal fall); then two more water-filled ditches and one dry one; and the finish was directly opposite the pavilion. But the race began not in the ring but two hundred yards out from it, and in that stretch of the course was the first obstacle, a dammed-up stream seven feet across, which the racers could leap or wade through, as they preferred.

Three times they were lined up to start, and each time one horse or another broke from the line, and they had to begin again. The starter, Colonel Sestrin, was starting to lose his temper, when at last for the fourth time he shouted "Away!" and the racers were off.
Every eye, every opera-glass, was turned on the brightly colored cluster of riders at the moment they were in line to start.
"They're off! They're starting!" went up on all sides after the hush of expectation.

And small groups and lone figures in the public began running from place to place to get a better view. In the very first moment the tight bunch of horsemen drew apart, and you could see them approaching the stream in twos and threes, one behind another. To the spectators it looked as if they had all started at the same instant, but for the racers there were seconds of difference that mattered a great deal.

Frou-Frou, jumpy and over-nervous, had missed the first moment, and several horses had started before her, but before reaching the stream Vronsky, holding the mare in with all his strength as she tugged at the bridle, easily overtook three of them, and was left with Mahotin's chestnut Gladiator in front of him, whose hindquarters were moving lightly and rhythmically up and down right ahead of Vronsky, and in front of all the dainty mare Diana carrying Kuzovlev more dead than alive.
For the first instant Vronsky was master neither of himself nor of his mare. Up to the first obstacle, the stream, he could not control her movements.

Gladiator and Diana came up to it together and almost at the same instant; together they rose above the stream and flew to the other side; Frou-Frou shot after them as if airborne; but at the very moment Vronsky felt himself in the air, he suddenly saw, almost beneath his mare's hoofs, Kuzovlev floundering on the far side of the stream with Diana. (Kuzovlev had let go of the reins as he took the leap, and the mare had thrown him over her head.) Vronsky learned the details later; at that moment all he saw was that, just below him, where Frou-Frou had to land, Diana's legs or head might be in the way. But Frou-Frou drew up her legs and back in the very act of jumping, like a falling cat, and, clearing the other mare, landed beyond her.
"Oh, the darling!" Vronsky thought.

After crossing the stream Vronsky had complete control of his mare and began holding her in, meaning to clear the big barrier behind Mahotin and to try to overtake him on the open stretch of about five hundred yards that came next.

The big barrier stood right in front of the imperial pavilion. The Tsar and the whole court and crowds of people were all watching them — at him, with Mahotin a length ahead, as they approached the "devil," as the solid barrier was called. Vronsky was aware of those eyes fastened on him from every side, but he saw nothing except the ears and neck of his own mare, the ground racing to meet him, and the back and white legs of Gladiator beating time swiftly in front of him, always at the same distance ahead. Gladiator rose, with no sound of striking anything. With a flick of his short tail he vanished from Vronsky's sight.
"Bravo!" cried a voice.

At that same moment, just beneath Vronsky's eyes, the palings of the barrier flashed by. With no change in her stride his mare flew over it; the palings disappeared, and he heard only a crash behind him. The mare, excited by Gladiator keeping ahead, had risen too early before the barrier and grazed it with her hind hoofs. But her pace never broke, and Vronsky, feeling a spatter of mud strike his face, realized he was once again the same distance from Gladiator. Once more he saw before him the same back and short tail, and again the same swiftly moving white legs that got no further away.

At the very moment Vronsky was thinking now was the time to overtake Mahotin, Frou-Frou herself, picking up on his thoughts without any prompting from him, gained ground considerably and began coming alongside Mahotin on the most favorable side, close to the inner rope. Mahotin wouldn't let her by on that side. Vronsky had barely formed the thought that he might pass on the outer side, when Frou-Frou shifted her stride and began overtaking him on the other side. Frou-Frou's shoulder, by now beginning to darken with sweat, was level with Gladiator's back. For a few lengths they ran even. But before the next obstacle they were approaching, Vronsky began working the reins, eager to avoid being forced to the outer circle, and swiftly passed Mahotin just at the dip. He caught a glimpse of his mud-spattered face as he flashed by. He even fancied that Mahotin smiled. Vronsky passed Mahotin, but he was immediately aware of him close behind, never ceasing to hear the even thud of hoofs and the rapid, still entirely fresh breathing of Gladiator.

The next two obstacles, the water course and the barrier, were easily cleared, but Vronsky began to hear Gladiator's snort and thud closer behind him. He urged his mare on, and to his delight felt her easily quicken her pace, and the thud of Gladiator's hoofs was again at the same distance away.

Vronsky was at the head of the race, just as he had wanted to be and as Cord had advised, and now he felt sure of being the winner. His excitement, his joy, his tenderness for Frou-Frou grew sharper and sharper. He longed to look back, but he didn't dare, and he tried to keep cool and not push his mare, so as to leave the same reserve of strength in her that he sensed Gladiator still had. Only one obstacle remained, the hardest one; if he could clear it ahead of the others he would come in first. He was flying toward the Irish barricade. Frou-Frou and he both saw the barricade in the distance, and both man and mare had a moment's hesitation. He saw the uncertainty in the mare's ears and lifted the whip, but at the same time felt his fears were groundless; the mare knew what was wanted. She quickened her stride and rose smoothly, just as he had imagined she would, and as she left the ground she gave herself up to the force of her surge, which carried her far beyond the ditch; and with the same rhythm, without effort, with the same leading leg, Frou-Frou settled back into her stride.

"Bravo, Vronsky!" he heard shouts from a knot of men — he knew they were his friends from the regiment — standing by the obstacle. He could not fail to recognize Yashvin's voice, though he did not see him.

"Oh, my sweet!" he said inwardly to Frou-Frou, listening for what was happening behind him. "He's cleared it!" he thought, catching the thud of Gladiator's hoofs behind him. Only the last ditch remained, filled with water and five feet across. Vronsky didn't even look at it, but, eager to come in well ahead, he began sawing at the reins, lifting the mare's head and letting it go in time with her pace. He felt that the mare was at her last reserve of strength; not just her neck and shoulders were wet, but sweat stood in drops on her mane, her head, her sharp ears, and her breath came in short, sharp gasps. But he knew she had strength more than enough for the remaining five hundred yards. It was only from the sense of being closer to the ground, and the peculiar smoothness of his motion, that Vronsky knew how much the mare had quickened her pace. She flew over the ditch as if not noticing it. She flew over it like a bird; but in that same instant Vronsky, to his horror, felt that he had failed to keep up with the mare's motion — that he had, he could not say how, made a fearful, unforgivable mistake in recovering his seat in the saddle. All at once his position had shifted and he knew something terrible had happened. He couldn't yet make out what, when the white legs of a chestnut horse flashed by close to him, and Mahotin shot past at a swift gallop. Vronsky was touching the ground with one foot, and his mare was sinking onto that foot. He just had time to free his leg before she fell on one side, gasping painfully, and, making vain efforts to rise with her delicate, soaking neck, she fluttered on the ground at his feet like a shot bird. The clumsy movement Vronsky had made had broken her back. But that he only learned much later. At that moment all he knew was that Mahotin had flown swiftly past, while he stood staggering alone on the muddy, motionless ground, with Frou-Frou lying gasping in front of him, bending her head back and gazing at him with her exquisite eyes. Still unable to grasp what had happened, Vronsky tugged at his mare's reins. Again she struggled all over like a fish, and her shoulders heaving against the saddle, she rose onto her forelegs but, unable to lift her back, she shuddered and again fell on her side. With a face hideous with passion, his lower jaw shaking and his cheeks white, Vronsky kicked her with his heel in the stomach and again tugged at the reins. She did not stir, but, thrusting her nose into the ground, simply gazed at her master with her speaking eyes.
"A-a-ah!" Vronsky groaned, clutching at his head. "Ah, what have I done!" he cried. "The race lost! And my fault! Shameful, unforgivable! And the poor darling, ruined mare! Ah — what have I done!"

A crowd of men, a doctor and his assistant, the officers of his regiment, ran up to him. To his misery he felt that he was whole and unhurt. The mare had broken her back, and it was decided to shoot her. Vronsky could not answer questions, could not speak to anyone. He turned, and, without picking up his cap that had fallen off, walked away from the racecourse with no idea where he was going. He felt utterly wretched. For the first time in his life he had come to know the bitterest sort of misfortune — misfortune past mending, and caused by his own fault.

Yashvin caught up with him with his cap, and led him home; and half an hour later Vronsky had pulled himself together. But the memory of that race stayed in his heart for a long time, the cruelest and bitterest memory of his life.

title: Chapter 26
paragraphs: The outward relations of Alexey Alexandrovitch and his wife had not changed. The only difference was that he was busier than ever. As in earlier years, he had gone abroad at the start of spring to a foreign watering place for the sake of his health, which was strained each year by the winter's work that grew heavier and heavier. And, as always, he returned in July and at once threw himself into work with even greater energy. As usual, too, his wife had moved out of town for the summer to a villa, while he remained in Petersburg. From the date of their conversation after the party at Princess Tverskaya's he had never again spoken to Anna of his suspicions and jealousy, and that habitual tone of mocking mimicry was the most convenient possible for his present attitude toward his wife. He was a little colder to her. He seemed merely a little put out with her over that first midnight conversation, which she had brushed aside. In his manner toward her there was a shade of vexation, but nothing more. "You wouldn't be open with me," he seemed to be telling her in his mind; "so much the worse for you. Now you may beg as much as you like, but I will not be open with you. So much the worse for you!" he said inwardly, like a man who, having vainly tried to put out a fire, flies into a rage at his own useless efforts and says, "Oh, very well then — you can burn for this!" This man, so subtle and shrewd in official life, did not realize all the senselessness of such an attitude toward his wife. He did not realize it because it was too terrible for him to grasp his real position, and he had shut down and locked and sealed up in his heart that secret place where his feelings about his family — that is, his wife and son — lay hidden. He, who had been such a careful father, had grown peculiarly cold to his son from the end of that winter on, and adopted toward him the same bantering tone he used with his wife. "Aha, young man!" was the greeting with which he met him.

Alexey Alexandrovitch asserted, and believed, that he had never in any previous year had so much official business as that year. But he was not aware that he was seeking out work for himself that year — that this was one of the means of keeping shut that secret place where his feelings about his wife and son and his thoughts about them lay hidden, growing more terrible the longer they lay there. If anyone had had the right to ask Alexey Alexandrovitch what he thought of his wife's behavior, the mild and peaceable Alexey Alexandrovitch would have given no answer, but he would have been deeply angered with anyone who put the question to him. For this reason there came into Alexey Alexandrovitch's face a look of haughtiness and severity whenever anyone inquired after his wife's health. Alexey Alexandrovitch did not want to think at all about his wife's behavior, and he actually succeeded in not thinking about it at all.

Alexey Alexandrovitch's permanent summer villa was in Peterhof, and Countess Lidia Ivanovna usually spent the summer there, close to Anna, and constantly in her company. That year Countess Lidia Ivanovna declined to settle in Peterhof, did not come to see Anna Arkadyevna once, and, in conversation with Alexey Alexandrovitch, hinted at the unsuitability of Anna's close intimacy with Betsy and Vronsky. Alexey Alexandrovitch cut her short sharply, declaring outright that his wife was above suspicion, and from that time on he began to avoid Countess Lidia Ivanovna. He did not want to see, and did not see, that many people in society cast dubious glances at his wife; he did not want to understand, and did not understand, why his wife had so particularly insisted on staying at Tsarskoe, where Betsy was staying, and not far from the camp of Vronsky's regiment. He did not allow himself to think about it, and he did not think about it; and yet, although he never admitted it to himself and had no proofs, not even circumstantial ones, in the bottom of his heart he knew beyond all doubt that he was a deceived husband, and he was profoundly miserable about it.

How often during those eight years of happy life with his wife had Alexey Alexandrovitch looked at other men's unfaithful wives and other deceived husbands and asked himself: "How can people sink to that? How is it they don't put an end to such a hideous position?" But now, when the misfortune had come upon himself, he was so far from thinking of putting an end to the position that he refused to acknowledge it at all — refused precisely because it was too awful, too unnatural.
