Since his return from abroad Alexey Alexandrovitch had been at their country villa twice. Once he dined there, and another time he spent the evening there with a party of friends, but he had not once stayed the night there, as had been his habit in previous years.

The day of the races was a very busy one for Alexey Alexandrovitch; but when he was mentally planning out the day that morning, he had decided to go to their country house to see his wife immediately after dinner, and from there to the races, which the whole court would be attending and at which he was obliged to be present. He was going to see his wife because he had made up his mind to see her once a week to keep up appearances. And besides, on that day, being the fifteenth, he had to give his wife some money for her expenses, according to their usual arrangement.
With his habitual control over his thoughts, although he thought all this about his wife, he did not let his thoughts wander any further with regard to her.

That morning was a very full one for Alexey Alexandrovitch. The evening before, Countess Lidia Ivanovna had sent him a pamphlet by a celebrated traveler in China, who was staying in Petersburg, and with it a note begging him to see the traveler in person, as he was an extremely interesting man from various angles and likely to be of use. Alexey Alexandrovitch had not had time to read the pamphlet through in the evening, and finished it in the morning. Then people began arriving with petitions, and came the reports, the interviews, the appointments, the dismissals, the apportionment of rewards, pensions, grants, notes — the workaday round, as Alexey Alexandrovitch called it, that always ate up so much time. Then there was private business of his own — a visit from the doctor and from the steward who managed his property. The steward did not take long. He simply handed Alexey Alexandrovitch the money he needed along with a brief account of the state of his affairs, which was not altogether satisfactory, since it had happened that during that year, because of increased expenses, more had been paid out than usual, and there was a deficit. But the doctor, a celebrated Petersburg doctor who was an intimate acquaintance of Alexey Alexandrovitch's, took up a great deal of time. Alexey Alexandrovitch had not expected him that day, and was surprised at his visit, and even more so when the doctor questioned him very carefully about his health, listened to his breathing, and tapped at his liver. Alexey Alexandrovitch did not know that his friend Lidia Ivanovna, noticing that he was not as well as usual that year, had begged the doctor to go and examine him. "Do it for my sake," Countess Lidia Ivanovna had said to him.
"I will do it for the sake of Russia, countess," the doctor answered.
"A priceless man!" said Countess Lidia Ivanovna.

The doctor was extremely dissatisfied with Alexey Alexandrovitch. He found the liver considerably enlarged and the digestive powers weakened, while the course of mineral waters had been entirely without effect. He prescribed more physical exercise so far as possible, and as far as possible less mental strain, and above all no worry — in other words, just what was as much out of Alexey Alexandrovitch's power as abstaining from breathing. Then he withdrew, leaving Alexey Alexandrovitch with an uncomfortable sense that something was wrong with him, and that there was no chance of curing it.

As he was leaving, the doctor happened to meet on the staircase an acquaintance of his, Sludin, the secretary of Alexey Alexandrovitch's department. They had been comrades at the university, and though they rarely met, they thought highly of each other and were excellent friends, and so there was no one to whom the doctor would have given his opinion of a patient as freely as to Sludin.
"How glad I am you've been seeing him!" said Sludin. "He's not well, and I think.... Well, what's your verdict?"

"I'll tell you," said the doctor, beckoning over Sludin's head to his coachman to bring the carriage round. "It's like this," the doctor said, taking a finger of his kid glove in his white hands and pulling on it, "if you don't strain the strings and then try to break them, you'll find it a hard job; but strain a string to its very limit, and the mere weight of one finger on the strained string will snap it. And with his close attention to detail, his conscientious devotion to his work, he's strained to the limit; and there's some outside burden weighing on him, and not a light one," the doctor concluded, raising his eyebrows significantly. "Will you be at the races?" he added as he sank into his seat in the carriage.
"Yes, yes, of course; it does waste a lot of time," the doctor answered vaguely to some remark from Sludin he hadn't caught.

Right after the doctor, who had taken up so much time, came the celebrated traveler, and Alexey Alexandrovitch, with the help of the pamphlet he had only just finished reading and his previous familiarity with the subject, impressed the traveler with the depth of his knowledge and the breadth and enlightenment of his view of it.

At the same time as the traveler, a provincial marshal of nobility on a visit to Petersburg was announced, and Alexey Alexandrovitch had to have some conversation with him. After his departure, Alexey Alexandrovitch had to finish the daily routine of business with his secretary, and then he still had to drive over to call on a certain great personage on a matter of grave and serious import. Alexey Alexandrovitch only just managed to be back by five o'clock, his dinner hour, and after dining with his secretary he invited him to drive with him to his country villa and to the races.
Though he did not admit it to himself, Alexey Alexandrovitch was now always trying to secure the presence of a third person in his meetings with his wife.

title: Chapter 27
paragraphs: Anna was upstairs, standing before the looking glass, and, with Annushka's help, pinning the last ribbon on her gown when she heard carriage wheels crunching the gravel at the entrance.

"It's too early for Betsy," she thought, and, glancing out of the window, she caught sight of the carriage and Alexey Alexandrovitch's black hat, with the ears she knew so well sticking up on either side of it. "How unlucky! Can he be planning to stay the night?" she wondered, and the thought of all that might come of such a chance struck her as so awful and terrifying that, without dwelling on it for an instant, she went down to meet him with a bright, radiant face; and, aware of the presence of that spirit of falsehood and deceit in herself that she had come to know lately, she gave herself over to it and began chattering, hardly knowing what she was saying.

"Ah, how kind of you!" she said, giving her husband her hand, and greeting Sludin, who was like one of the family, with a smile. "You're staying the night, I hope?" was the first thing the spirit of falsehood prompted her to say; "and now we'll go together. Only it's a pity I've promised Betsy. She's coming to fetch me."
Alexey Alexandrovitch frowned at the mention of Betsy's name.

"Oh, I'm not going to separate the inseparables," he said in his usual mocking tone. "I'll go with Mihail Vassilievitch. The doctors have ordered me exercise too. I'll walk, and imagine myself back at the springs."
"There's no hurry," said Anna. "Would you like some tea?"
She rang.

"Bring tea, and let Seryozha know that Alexey Alexandrovitch is here. So — tell me, how have things been? Mihail Vassilievitch, this is your first time visiting me. Just look how lovely it is out there on the terrace," she said, turning to one of them and then the other in turn.

She spoke very simply and naturally, but too much and too fast. She was the more aware of it because she noticed in the inquisitive look Mihail Vassilievitch turned on her that he was, in effect, keeping watch on her.
Mihail Vassilievitch promptly went out onto the terrace.
She sat down beside her husband.
"You don't look quite well," she said.
"Yes," he said; "the doctor came round today and wasted an hour of my time. I get the feeling one of our friends sent him: my health, it seems, is so precious."
"No — what did he say?"
She asked him about his health and what he had been doing, and tried to persuade him to take a rest and come out to her.

All this she said brightly, rapidly, and with a peculiar brilliance in her eyes. But Alexey Alexandrovitch attached no special significance now to this tone of hers. He heard only her words and gave them only the plain sense they bore. And he answered simply, though jestingly. There was nothing remarkable in this whole conversation, but Anna could never afterward recall this brief scene without an agonizing pang of shame.

Seryozha came in led by his governess. Had Alexey Alexandrovitch allowed himself to observe, he would have noticed the timid, bewildered eyes with which Seryozha glanced first at his father and then at his mother. But he wouldn't see anything, and he didn't see it.
"Ah, the young man! He's grown. Really, he's becoming quite a man. How are you, young man?"

And he held out his hand to the frightened child. Seryozha had always been shy of his father, and now, ever since Alexey Alexandrovitch had taken to calling him young man, and since that unsolvable question had come into his head whether Vronsky was a friend or a foe, he avoided his father. He looked around toward his mother as though seeking shelter. Only with his mother was he at ease. Meanwhile Alexey Alexandrovitch was holding his son by the shoulder while he spoke to the governess, and Seryozha was so miserably uncomfortable that Anna could see he was on the verge of tears.

Anna, who had flushed a little the instant her son came in, noticing that Seryozha was uncomfortable, got up hurriedly, lifted Alexey Alexandrovitch's hand from her son's shoulder, and, kissing the boy, led him out onto the terrace and quickly came back.
"But it's time to start," she said, glancing at her watch. "How is it that Betsy hasn't come?..."

"Yes," said Alexey Alexandrovitch, and, getting up, he folded his hands and cracked his fingers. "I've come to bring you some money too, since nightingales, we know, can't live on fairy tales," he said. "You need some, I expect?"
"No, I don't... yes, I do," she said, not looking at him, and reddening to the roots of her hair. "But you'll come back here after the races, I suppose?"

"Oh, yes!" Alexey Alexandrovitch answered. "And here's the glory of Peterhof, Princess Tverskaya," he added, looking out the window at the elegant English carriage with the tiny seats placed extremely high. "What elegance! Charming! Well — let's get going too, then."
Princess Tverskaya did not get out of her carriage, but her groom — in tall boots, a cape, and a black hat — sprang out at the entrance.
"I'm going; goodbye!" Anna said, and, kissing her son, she went up to Alexey Alexandrovitch and held out her hand to him. "It was ever so kind of you to come."
Alexey Alexandrovitch kissed her hand.

"Well, _au revoir_, then! You'll come back for some tea; that's lovely!" she said, and she went out, gay and radiant. But the moment she could no longer see him, she became aware of the spot on her hand where his lips had touched, and she shuddered with revulsion.

title: Chapter 28
paragraphs: By the time Alexey Alexandrovitch reached the racecourse, Anna was already sitting in the pavilion next to Betsy — the pavilion where all the highest society had gathered. She spotted her husband from a distance. Two men, her husband and her lover, were the two centers of her existence, and without help from her outward senses she felt their nearness. She was aware of her husband approaching from a long way off, and could not help following him through the surging crowd in the middle of which he was moving. She watched his progress toward the pavilion, saw him now answering an ingratiating bow with condescension, now exchanging friendly, casual greetings with his equals, now diligently trying to catch the eye of one of this world's great ones, and taking off his big round hat that squeezed the tops of his ears. All these mannerisms of his she knew, and all of them were hateful to her. "Nothing but ambition, nothing but the wish to get on — that's all there is in his soul," she thought; "as for these lofty ideals, love of culture, religion — they're only so many tools for getting on."

From his glances toward the ladies' pavilion (he was staring straight at her, but did not distinguish his wife in the sea of muslin, ribbons, feathers, parasols and flowers) she saw he was looking for her, but she deliberately avoided noticing him.
"Alexey Alexandrovitch!" Princess Betsy called to him; "I'm sure you don't see your wife: here she is."
He smiled his chilly smile.

"There's so much splendor here that one's eyes are dazzled," he said, and he stepped into the pavilion. He smiled at his wife as a man ought to smile on meeting his wife after just parting from her, and greeted the princess and other acquaintances, giving each one what was their due — that is, jesting with the ladies and dealing out friendly greetings among the men. Below, near the pavilion, was standing an adjutant general of whom Alexey Alexandrovitch had a high opinion, noted for his intelligence and culture. Alexey Alexandrovitch struck up a conversation with him.

There was an interval between races, so nothing got in the way of conversation. The adjutant general expressed his disapproval of racing. Alexey Alexandrovitch replied, defending it. Anna heard his high, measured tones, not missing a word, and every word struck her as false and stabbed her ears with pain.

When the three-mile steeplechase was about to begin, she bent forward and watched, with fixed eyes, Vronsky as he went up to his horse and mounted, while at the same time she heard that loathsome, never-ceasing voice of her husband. She was in an agony of terror for Vronsky, but a still greater agony was the never-ceasing, as it seemed to her, stream of her husband's shrill voice with its familiar intonations.

"I'm a wicked woman, a lost woman," she thought; "but I don't like lying, I can't bear falsehood — while for _him_ (her husband) it's the very breath of life. He knows all about it, he sees everything; what does he care if he can talk so calmly? If he were to kill me, if he were to kill Vronsky, I might respect him. No — all he wants is falsehood and propriety," Anna said to herself, not considering exactly what she wanted from her husband, or how she would have liked to see him behave. She did not understand, either, that Alexey Alexandrovitch's peculiar loquacity that day, so maddening to her, was simply the expression of his inward distress and unease. As a child who has been hurt skips about, throwing all his muscles into motion to drown out the pain, in the same way Alexey Alexandrovitch needed mental exercise to drown out the thoughts of his wife that, in her presence and Vronsky's, with the continual repetition of his name, kept forcing themselves on his attention. And it was as natural for him to talk well and cleverly as it is natural for a child to skip about. He was saying:

"Danger in the races of officers, of cavalrymen, is an essential element of the race. If England can point to the most brilliant feats of cavalry in military history, it is simply because she has historically developed this force, both in beasts and in men. Sport, in my opinion, has great value, and as always we see only what is most superficial."
"It's not superficial," said Princess Tverskaya. "One of the officers, they say, has broken two ribs."
Alexey Alexandrovitch smiled his smile, which uncovered his teeth and revealed nothing more.

"We'll grant, princess, that that's not superficial," he said, "but internal. But that's not the point," and he turned again to the general with whom he had been speaking seriously; "we mustn't forget that those taking part in the race are military men, who have chosen that career, and one must admit that every calling has its disagreeable side. It forms an integral part of an officer's duties. Low sports, such as prize-fighting or Spanish bullfights, are a sign of barbarity. But specialized trials of skill are a sign of development."
"No, I won't come another time; it's too upsetting," said Princess Betsy. "Isn't it, Anna?"
"It is upsetting — but one can't tear oneself away," said another lady. "If I'd been a Roman woman I should never have missed a single circus."
Anna said nothing, and, keeping her opera-glass raised, gazed always at the same spot.
Just then a tall general passed through the pavilion. Cutting off what he was in the middle of saying, Alexey Alexandrovitch rose quickly — though still with dignity — and made a low bow to him.
"You're not racing?" the officer asked, teasing him.
"My race is a harder one," Alexey Alexandrovitch answered deferentially.
And though the reply meant nothing, the general looked as if he had heard a witty remark from a witty man, and thoroughly relished _la pointe de la sauce_.

"There are two aspects," Alexey Alexandrovitch resumed: "those who take part and those who watch; and love for such spectacles is an unmistakable proof of a low degree of development in the spectator, I admit, but...."
"Princess, bets!" came Stepan Arkadyevitch's voice from below, calling up to Betsy. "Who's your favorite?"
"Anna and I are for Kuzovlev," Betsy answered.
"I'm for Vronsky. A pair of gloves?"
"Done!"
"But it is a pretty sight, isn't it?"
Alexey Alexandrovitch paused while there was talk going on around him, but he started up again at once.
"I admit that manly sports do not...." he was continuing.

But at that moment the racers started, and all conversation broke off. Alexey Alexandrovitch fell silent too, and everyone stood up and turned toward the stream. Alexey Alexandrovitch had no interest in the race, and so he did not watch the racers, but began listlessly to scan the spectators with his weary eyes. His gaze rested on Anna.

Her face was white and set. She was clearly seeing nothing and no one but one man. Her hand had clutched her fan convulsively, and she was holding her breath. He looked at her and hastily turned away, scanning other faces.

"Well, here's this lady too, and others equally moved; it's perfectly natural," Alexey Alexandrovitch told himself. He tried not to look at her, but unconsciously his eyes were drawn back to her. He examined that face again, trying not to read what was so plainly written on it, and against his own will, with horror, read on it what he did not want to know.

The first fall — Kuzovlev's, at the stream — agitated everyone, but Alexey Alexandrovitch saw distinctly on Anna's pale, triumphant face that the man she was watching had not fallen. When, after Mahotin and Vronsky had cleared the worst barrier, the next officer was thrown straight onto his head at it and fatally injured, and a shudder of horror ran through the whole crowd, Alexey Alexandrovitch saw that Anna did not even notice it, and had some trouble making out what they were talking about around her. But more and more often, and with increasing persistence, he watched her. Anna, wholly absorbed in the race as she was, became aware of her husband's cold eyes fixed on her from one side.
She glanced round for an instant, looked at him questioningly, and, with a slight frown, turned away again.
"Ah, I don't care!" she seemed to be saying to him, and she did not look at him again once.

The race was an unlucky one, and of the seventeen officers who rode in it more than half were thrown and hurt. By the end everyone was in a state of agitation, which was made all the worse by the fact that the Tsar was displeased.

title: Chapter 29
paragraphs: Everyone was loudly expressing their disapproval, everyone was repeating a phrase someone had uttered — "The lions and gladiators will be next" — and everyone was feeling horrified; so that when Vronsky fell to the ground, and Anna moaned aloud, there was nothing very out of the ordinary in it. But then a change came over Anna's face that really was beyond decorum. She utterly lost her head. She began fluttering like a caged bird, one moment about to get up and move away, the next turning to Betsy.
"Let us go, let us go!" she said.
But Betsy didn't hear her. She was leaning down, talking to a general who had come up to her.
Alexey Alexandrovitch went up to Anna and politely offered her his arm.
"Let us go, if you like," he said in French, but Anna was listening to the general and did not notice her husband.
"He's broken his leg too, they say," the general was saying. "This is beyond everything."

Without answering her husband, Anna lifted her opera-glass and gazed toward the spot where Vronsky had fallen; but it was so far away, and there was such a crowd of people around it, that she could make out nothing. She lowered the opera-glass and would have moved away, but at that moment an officer galloped up and made some announcement to the Tsar. Anna craned forward, listening.
"Stiva! Stiva!" she called to her brother.
But her brother did not hear her. Again she would have moved away.
"Once more I offer you my arm if you want to leave," said Alexey Alexandrovitch, reaching for her hand.
She drew back from him with revulsion, and without looking him in the face answered:
"No, no, let me be — I'll stay."

She could see now that an officer was running back across the course toward the pavilion from the spot where Vronsky had fallen. Betsy signaled to him with her handkerchief. When the officer reached them, he reported that the rider was unhurt, but that the horse had broken its back.

At this news Anna sank into her seat and buried her face in her fan. Alexey Alexandrovitch could see that she was weeping, unable to hold back her tears or even the sobs heaving in her chest. He positioned himself in front of her so as to screen her from the others, and let her gather herself.
"For the third time I offer you my arm," he said to her after a little while, turning to her. Anna looked at him and did not know what to say. Princess Betsy came to her rescue.
"No, Alexey Alexandrovitch; I brought Anna and I promised to take her home," put in Betsy.
"Excuse me, princess," he said, smiling courteously but looking her very firmly in the face, "but I can see Anna is not well, and I want her to come home with me."
Anna looked around her in a frightened way, got up submissively, and laid her hand on her husband's arm.
"I'll send to find out about him and let you know," Betsy whispered to her.

As they left the pavilion, Alexey Alexandrovitch, as always, spoke to those he met, and Anna had, as always, to talk and answer; but she was completely beside herself, and moved on her husband's arm as if in a dream.
"Is he killed or not? Is it true? Will he come or not? Shall I see him today?" she was thinking.

She took her seat in her husband's carriage in silence, and in silence they drove out of the crowd of carriages. In spite of everything he had seen, Alexey Alexandrovitch still would not let himself consider his wife's real condition. He saw only the outward symptoms. He saw that she had behaved improperly, and considered it his duty to tell her so. But it was very difficult for him not to say more — to tell her only that and nothing else. He opened his mouth to tell her she had behaved improperly, but he couldn't help saying something completely different.
"What an inclination we all have, though, for these cruel spectacles," he said. "I observe...."
"Eh? I don't understand," Anna said contemptuously.
He was offended, and at once started to say what he had meant to say.
"I am obliged to tell you," he began.
"So now we're going to have it out," she thought, and she felt frightened.
"I am obliged to tell you that your behavior today has been unbecoming," he said to her in French.

"In what way has my behavior been unbecoming?" she said aloud, turning her head sharply and looking him straight in the face — not with the bright expression that seemed to be covering something, but with a look of determination, beneath which she was barely concealing her dismay.
"Mind," he said, pointing to the open window opposite the coachman.
He got up and pulled up the window.
"What did you consider unbecoming?" she repeated.
"The despair you couldn't conceal at the accident to one of the riders."
He waited for her to answer, but she was silent, staring straight ahead.

"I've already asked you to conduct yourself in society in such a way that even malicious tongues can find nothing to say against you. There was a time when I spoke of your inward attitude, but I'm not speaking of that now. Now I speak only of your outward conduct. You have behaved improperly, and I want it not to happen again."

She did not hear half of what he was saying; she felt panic-stricken in front of him, and was wondering whether it was true that Vronsky had not been killed. Was it him they had meant when they said the rider was unhurt but the horse had broken its back? She merely smiled with pretended irony when he finished, and made no reply, because she had not heard what he said. Alexey Alexandrovitch had begun to speak boldly, but as he realized clearly what he was speaking of, the dismay she was feeling infected him too. He saw the smile, and a strange misapprehension came over him.
"She's smiling at my suspicions. Yes, she's going to tell me right now what she told me before — that there's no foundation for my suspicions, that it's absurd."

At that moment, when the revelation of everything was hanging over him, there was nothing he wanted so much as for her to answer mockingly, as before, that his suspicions were absurd and utterly without foundation. So terrible to him was what he knew that he was now ready to believe anything. But the look on her face — frightened and grim — did not now promise even a denial.
"Possibly I was mistaken," he said. "If so, I beg your pardon."

"No, you were not mistaken," she said with slow deliberation, staring in desperation into his cold face. "You weren't mistaken at all. I was in despair, and I couldn't help being so. I hear what you're saying, but it's him I'm thinking of. I love him; I am his mistress; I can't bear you; I'm afraid of you; I hate you.... Do with me whatever you please."

And dropping back into the corner of the carriage, she broke into sobs, hiding her face in her hands. Alexey Alexandrovitch did not stir, and kept staring straight ahead. But his whole face suddenly took on the solemn rigidity of the dead, and that expression did not change for the whole drive home. As they reached the house, he turned his head to her, still wearing the same expression.
"Very well! But I expect strict observance of the outward forms of propriety, until such time" — his voice shook — "as I may take measures to secure my honor and inform you of them."

He got out first and helped her down. In front of the servants he pressed her hand, took his seat in the carriage, and drove back to Petersburg. Right after, a footman came from Princess Betsy and brought Anna a note.
"I sent word to Alexey to find out how he is, and he writes that he is quite well and unhurt, but in despair."
"So _he_ will be coming," she thought. "What a good thing I told him everything!"
She glanced at her watch. She still had three hours to wait, and the memory of their last meeting set her blood on fire.
"My God, how light it is! It's dreadful, but I do love to see his face, and I do love this fantastic light.... My husband! Oh — yes.... Well, thank God! It's all over with him."

title: Chapter 30
paragraphs: At the little German spa where the Shtcherbatskys had settled — as in every place where people gather — the usual process of social crystallization went on, assigning every member a fixed and unalterable spot. Just as a particle of water in a frost locks itself into the precise form of a snow crystal, each new arrival at the springs was at once slotted into the place that fit them.
_Fürst_ Shtcherbatsky, _sammt Gemahlin und Tochter_, were immediately crystallized into a definite place — set there by the rooms they had taken, by their name, and by the company they fell in with.

That season a real German Fürstin happened to be visiting the spa, and the crystallizing process ran more briskly than ever. Princess Shtcherbatskaya wanted above all to present her daughter to this German princess, and the day after they arrived she duly carried out the ceremony. Kitty made a low, graceful curtsey in the _very simple_ — that is, very elegant — frock that had been ordered for her from Paris. The German princess said, "I hope the roses will soon come back to this pretty little face," and from that moment certain unbreakable lines were laid down for the Shtcherbatskys. They also got to know the family of an English Lady Somebody, a German countess and her son who had been wounded in the last war, a learned Swede, and M. Canut and his sister. But inevitably the Shtcherbatskys spent most of their time with a Moscow lady, Marya Yevgenyevna Rtishtcheva, and her daughter — whom Kitty disliked because she had fallen ill, like Kitty herself, over a love affair — along with a Moscow colonel Kitty had known since childhood, always seen until then in uniform and epaulettes, and now, with his little eyes, open neck, and flowered cravat, uncommonly ridiculous and tiresome, all the more because there was no shaking him off. Once the social pattern had set this firmly, Kitty grew badly bored, especially after the prince went away to Carlsbad and she was left alone with her mother. The people she already knew held no interest for her — nothing fresh would come of them. Her main entertainment at the spa became watching the people she did not know and inventing theories about them. It was characteristic of Kitty that she always pictured everyone in the best possible light, and never more so than with strangers. As she guessed at who people were, how they were connected, and what they were really like, she gave them the most extraordinary and noble characters, and then found confirmation of her guesses in everything she observed.

Of all these strangers, the one who attracted her most was a Russian girl who had come to the spa with an invalid Russian lady, Madame Stahl, as everyone called her. Madame Stahl belonged to the highest society, but she was so ill that she could not walk, and only on the rare fine day appeared at the springs in an invalid carriage. According to Princess Shtcherbatskaya, it was less her health than her pride that had kept Madame Stahl from making the acquaintance of any of the Russians there. The Russian girl looked after Madame Stahl, and Kitty noticed that she was also on easy terms with all the seriously ill people at the springs — and there were many of them — caring for them in the most unaffected way. The girl, as far as Kitty could gather, was not related to Madame Stahl, nor was she a paid attendant. Madame Stahl called her Varenka, and other people called her "Mademoiselle Varenka." Setting aside Kitty's curiosity about the girl's connection with Madame Stahl and with the other strangers, Kitty — as so often happened — felt herself drawn to Mademoiselle Varenka in a way she could not explain, and could tell when their eyes met that the feeling was mutual.

You could not quite say of Mademoiselle Varenka that she was past her first youth — she was more like a creature without youth at all; you might have taken her for nineteen or for thirty. Looked at feature by feature, she was handsome rather than plain, despite the sickly tinge of her face. Her figure would have been good too, if she had not been so painfully thin and her head so large for her medium height. Still, she was unlikely to attract men. She was like a fine flower already past its bloom and without fragrance, though its petals were not yet wilted. And she lacked precisely what Kitty had in such excess — the suppressed fire of vitality, the awareness of her own attractiveness.

She always seemed busy with work she could not possibly doubt the value of, and so seemed unable to be interested in anything outside it. That contrast with her own situation was exactly what made Mademoiselle Varenka so compelling to Kitty. Kitty felt that in her, in her whole way of life, she would find the example of what she was now so painfully searching for: an interest in life, a dignity in living — something quite apart from the social dealings between girls and men that now revolted her and looked to her like the shameless hawking of goods in search of a buyer. The more closely Kitty watched her unknown friend, the more convinced she became that this girl was the perfect creature she imagined, and the more eagerly she wanted to meet her.

The two girls passed each other several times a day, and each time Kitty's eyes were saying: "Who are you? What are you? Are you really the lovely creature I imagine? But please don't think," her eyes added, "that I would push myself on you — I simply admire you and like you." "I like you too, and you're very, very sweet. And I'd like you even more if I had the time," the eyes of the unknown girl answered. Kitty could see that she was always busy: taking the children of a Russian family home from the springs, fetching a shawl for a sick lady and tucking her into it, trying to amuse some peevish invalid, or choosing and buying cakes for someone's tea.

Soon after the Shtcherbatskys arrived, two new figures appeared in the morning crowd at the springs and drew universal — unfavorable — attention. There was a tall, stooping man with huge hands, dressed in an old coat too short for him, with black, plain, and yet alarming eyes; and a pockmarked, kind-faced woman, very badly and tastelessly dressed. Once Kitty recognized them as Russians, she had already begun, in her imagination, to spin a touching romance about them. But the princess, after consulting the visitors' register, found that this was Nikolay Levin with Marya Nikolaevna, and explained to Kitty what a bad man this Levin was — and all Kitty's fancies about the pair evaporated. It was less what her mother said than the fact that this was Konstantin's brother that made the two suddenly seem intensely unpleasant to Kitty. With his constant twitching of his head, Levin now provoked in her an uncontrollable feeling of disgust.
It seemed to her that his huge, terrible eyes, which kept following her, were full of hatred and contempt, and she tried to avoid crossing his path.

title: Chapter 31
paragraphs: It was a wet day. Rain had been falling all morning, and the invalids, parasols up, had crowded into the arcades.

Kitty was walking there with her mother and the Moscow colonel — smart and jaunty in his European coat, picked up ready-made in Frankfurt. They kept to one side of the arcade, trying to avoid Levin, who was walking down the other. Varenka, in her dark dress and a black hat with a turned-down brim, paced the whole length of the arcade with a blind Frenchwoman, and each time she passed Kitty they exchanged friendly looks.
"Mamma, couldn't I speak to her?" Kitty said, watching her unknown friend and noticing that she was heading toward the spring, where they might reach it at the same time.

"Oh, if you want to so badly, let me find out about her first and make her acquaintance myself," her mother answered. "What is it you see in her? She must be a paid companion. If you like, I'll introduce myself to Madame Stahl — I used to know her _belle-sœur_," the princess added, lifting her head loftily.
Kitty knew that the princess had taken offense at the way Madame Stahl had seemed to avoid meeting her. Kitty did not press the point.
"How wonderfully sweet she is!" she said, watching Varenka just as she handed a glass to the Frenchwoman. "Look how natural it all is, how kind."

"Your _engouements_ are so funny to watch," said the princess. "No — let's turn back," she added, spotting Levin coming toward them with his companion and a German doctor, all three talking very loudly and angrily.

They were turning back when suddenly they heard, not talk, but shouting. Levin had stopped short and was yelling at the doctor, and the doctor was shouting too. A crowd was gathering. The princess and Kitty beat a hasty retreat, while the colonel pushed into the crowd to find out what had happened.
A few minutes later the colonel caught up with them.
"What happened?" the princess asked.

"A scandal — disgraceful!" the colonel answered. "The one thing one dreads abroad is running into Russians. That tall man was abusing the doctor, throwing every kind of insult at him because he wasn't treating him the way he wanted, and then he started waving his stick at him. It's simply a scandal!"
"Oh, how unpleasant!" said the princess. "And how did it end?"
"Luckily at that point that — the one in the mushroom hat — stepped in. A Russian lady, I think," said the colonel.
"Mademoiselle Varenka?" Kitty asked.
"Yes, yes. She came to the rescue before anyone else; she took the man by the arm and led him away."
"There, mamma," said Kitty. "You wonder that I'm so enthusiastic about her."

The next day, watching her unknown friend, Kitty saw that Mademoiselle Varenka was already on the same terms with Levin and his companion as with her other _protégés_. She went up to them, fell into conversation with them, and acted as interpreter for the woman, who could not speak a foreign language.

Kitty began begging her mother even more urgently to let her make friends with Varenka. And disagreeable as it was for the princess to seem to be the first to seek out Madame Stahl, who was apparently giving herself airs, she made inquiries about Varenka and, finding that the acquaintance could do no harm even if it did little good, she approached Varenka herself and introduced herself.
Choosing a moment when her daughter had gone off to the spring and Varenka had paused outside the baker's, the princess went up to her.
"Allow me to introduce myself," she said with her dignified smile. "My daughter has lost her heart to you," she said. "You may not know who I am. I am — "
"That feeling is more than mutual, princess," Varenka answered quickly.
"What a kind thing you did yesterday for our poor compatriot!" the princess said.
Varenka flushed a little. "I don't remember. I don't think I did anything," she said.
"Why, you saved that Levin from real trouble."
"Yes — _sa compagne_ called me over, and I tried to calm him down. He's very ill and was unhappy with the doctor. I'm used to looking after that kind of patient."
"Yes, I'd heard you live at Mentone with your aunt — I think — Madame Stahl. I used to know her _belle-sœur_."
"No, she isn't my aunt. I call her mamma, but I am not related to her; I was brought up by her," Varenka answered, coloring slightly again.
She said it so simply, and her face was so candid and truthful, that the princess saw at once why Kitty had taken such a fancy to Varenka.
"Well, and what is this Levin going to do?" the princess asked.
"He's leaving," Varenka answered.
At that moment Kitty came up from the spring, beaming because her mother had at last made her unknown friend's acquaintance.
"Well, you see, Kitty — your great desire to make friends with Mademoiselle —"
"Varenka," Varenka put in, smiling. "That's what everyone calls me."

Kitty blushed with pleasure and, slowly and silently, pressed her new friend's hand. The hand did not return the pressure but lay still in hers. Yet Mademoiselle Varenka's face lit up with a soft, glad, if rather sad smile that showed her large but handsome teeth.
"I have wanted this for a long time too," she said.
"But you're so busy."
"Oh, no — I'm not busy at all," Varenka answered, but at that very moment she had to leave her new friends: two little Russian girls, an invalid's children, came running up to her.
"Varenka, mamma's calling!" they cried.
And Varenka went off with them.

title: Chapter 32
paragraphs: What the princess had been able to learn about Varenka's past and her relations with Madame Stahl amounted to this:

Madame Stahl — of whom some said she had nagged her husband out of his life and others that he had made her wretched by his immoral behavior — had always been a woman of weak health and high enthusiasm. After her separation from her husband, when she gave birth to her only child, the baby died almost at once, and Madame Stahl's family, knowing how sensitive she was and afraid the news would kill her, swapped the dead baby for another one born the same night in the same house in Petersburg, the daughter of the chief cook of the Imperial Household. This was Varenka. Madame Stahl learned later that Varenka was not her own child, but she went on raising her as her own, especially since Varenka very soon had no blood relatives of her own left. Madame Stahl had now lived more than ten years continuously abroad, in the south, never leaving her couch. Some said Madame Stahl had built her social position as a philanthropic, deeply religious woman; others said she really was in her heart the highly ethical person living only for the good of her fellow creatures that she made herself out to be. No one knew what her faith was — Catholic, Protestant, or Orthodox. But one thing was beyond doubt: she was on friendly terms with the highest figures of every church and sect.
Varenka lived with her abroad the whole time, and everyone who knew Madame Stahl knew and liked Mademoiselle Varenka, as everyone called her.

Once she had learned all this, the princess could find no objection to her daughter's closeness with Varenka — all the more since Varenka's breeding and education were of the highest sort (she spoke French and English extremely well) and, what counted most, she brought a message from Madame Stahl expressing regret that her poor health prevented her from making the princess's acquaintance.
After getting to know Varenka, Kitty became more and more fascinated by her, and every day she found some new virtue in her.
Hearing that Varenka had a good voice, the princess asked her to come and sing for them in the evening.

"Kitty plays, and we have a piano — not a good one, it's true, but you'd give us so much pleasure," said the princess with her affected smile, which Kitty particularly disliked just then because she could see that Varenka had no inclination to sing. Still, Varenka came in the evening and brought a roll of music with her. The princess had also invited Marya Yevgenyevna and her daughter and the colonel.

Varenka seemed perfectly unbothered by the presence of strangers, and went straight to the piano. She could not accompany herself, but she could sing music at sight very well. Kitty, who played well, took the accompaniment.
"You have an extraordinary talent," the princess told her after Varenka had sung the first piece beautifully.
Marya Yevgenyevna and her daughter added their thanks and admiration.
"Look," said the colonel, glancing out of the window, "what an audience has gathered to listen to you." A considerable crowd really had collected under the windows.
"I'm so glad it gives you pleasure," Varenka answered simply.

Kitty looked proudly at her friend. She was enchanted by her talent, by her voice, by her face — but most of all by her manner, by the way Varenka clearly thought nothing of her own singing and was entirely unmoved by their praise. She seemed only to be asking: "Shall I sing more, or is that enough?"

"If it had been me," thought Kitty, "how proud I would have been! How delighted I would have been by that crowd under the windows! And she's untouched by it. Her one motive is not to refuse and to please mamma. What is in her? Where does she get the power to look down on all this, to be calm whatever happens? I would love to know it, to learn it from her!" Kitty thought, watching her serene face. The princess asked Varenka to sing again, and Varenka sang another song, just as smoothly, clearly, and well, standing erect at the piano and beating time on it with her thin, dark hand.
The next song in the book was an Italian one. Kitty played the opening bars and looked round at Varenka.
"Let's skip that," said Varenka, coloring a little. Kitty kept her eyes on Varenka's face, with a look of dismayed inquiry.
"Very well, the next one," she said quickly, turning the pages — sensing at once that something was bound up with the song.
"No," said Varenka with a smile, laying her hand on the music. "No, let's have that one." And she sang it just as quietly, just as coolly, just as well as the others.
When she had finished, they all thanked her again and went off to tea. Kitty and Varenka went out into the little garden next to the house.
"Am I right that you have some memory connected with that song?" Kitty said. "Don't tell me what it is," she added quickly, "just say if I'm right."
"No, why not? I'll tell you," Varenka said, and without waiting for an answer she went on: "Yes, it brings back memories — painful ones, once. I cared for someone, and I used to sing him that song."
Kitty stared, wide-eyed and silent, in sympathy.

"I cared for him, and he cared for me; but his mother was against it, and he married another girl. He lives not far from us now, and I see him sometimes. You didn't think I had a love story of my own, did you?" she said, and there was a faint flash in her handsome face of the fire that Kitty was sure must once have glowed all over her.

"Didn't think so? Why — if I were a man, I could never care for anyone else after knowing you. Only I can't understand how he could forget you just to please his mother, and let you be unhappy. He had no heart."
"Oh, no, he's a very good man, and I'm not unhappy — quite the opposite, I'm very happy. Well, so we won't sing any more this evening," she added, turning back toward the house.
"How good you are! How good you are!" cried Kitty, and stopping her, she kissed her. "If only I could be even a little like you!"
"Why should you want to be like anyone? You're lovely as you are," Varenka said with her gentle, tired smile.

"No, I'm not lovely at all. Come, tell me — wait, sit down," said Kitty, pulling her down beside her again. "Tell me — isn't it humiliating to think that a man has rejected your love, that he didn't want it?"
"But he didn't reject it. I believe he cared for me — only he was an obedient son — "

"Yes, but suppose it hadn't been because of his mother — suppose it had been his own choice?" said Kitty, feeling she was giving away her own secret, and that her face, hot with shame, had already betrayed her.
"In that case he would have been in the wrong, and I wouldn't have regretted him," Varenka answered, clearly seeing that they were no longer talking about her, but about Kitty.
"But the humiliation," said Kitty — "the humiliation you can never forget, can never forget," she repeated, remembering the look she had given at the last ball, during the pause in the music.
"Where's the humiliation in it? You did nothing wrong."
"Worse than wrong — shameful."
Varenka shook her head and laid her hand on Kitty's.
"What's shameful about it?" she said. "You didn't tell a man who didn't care for you that you loved him, did you?"
"Of course not — I never said a word, but he knew. No, no — there are looks, there are ways. I won't forget it if I live a hundred years."
"Why on earth not? I don't understand. The whole question is whether you love him now or not," said Varenka, who called everything by its name.
"I hate him. I can't forgive myself."
"For what?"
"The shame, the humiliation!"
"Oh! If everyone were as sensitive as you are!" said Varenka. "There isn't a girl who hasn't gone through the same thing. And none of it matters."
"Then what does matter?" said Kitty, looking into her face with curious wonder.
"Oh, so many things matter," Varenka said, smiling.
"What, though?"

"Oh, so much that's more important," Varenka answered, not knowing quite what to say. But at that moment they heard the princess's voice from the window. "Kitty, it's cold! Either get a shawl, or come inside."
"It really is time to go in!" Varenka said, getting up. "I have to stop at Madame Berthe's — she asked me to."

Kitty held her by the hand, and her eyes, with passionate curiosity and pleading, asked: "What is it — what is this important thing that gives you such calm? Tell me, please!" But Varenka did not even know what Kitty's eyes were asking. She was simply thinking that she had to call on Madame Berthe that evening and then hurry home in time for _maman's_ tea at twelve. She went indoors, gathered up her music, and was saying goodbye to everyone when —
"Let me see you home," the colonel offered.
"Yes — you can't go alone at this hour," the princess chimed in. "I'll send Parasha with you, at least."
Kitty saw that Varenka could barely keep from smiling at the idea that she needed an escort.

"No, I always go about alone, and nothing ever happens to me," she said, taking her hat. And after one more kiss for Kitty — without ever saying what was important — she stepped out boldly with the music tucked under her arm and disappeared into the twilight of the summer night, carrying away with her the secret of what was important and what gave her the calm and dignity Kitty so envied.

title: Chapter 33
paragraphs: Kitty got to know Madame Stahl too, and this acquaintance, together with her friendship with Varenka, did more than influence her — it eased the distress she had been carrying. She found that comfort in a whole new world being opened to her through this meeting, a world with nothing in common with her past — a lofty, noble world from whose height she could look back on her past calmly. It was revealed to her that besides the instinctive life she had been giving herself up to until then, there was a spiritual life. This life was disclosed in religion, but a religion with nothing in common with the one Kitty had known since childhood, the one expressed in litanies and all-night services at the Widow's Home, where one could meet one's friends, or in memorizing Slavonic texts with the priest. This was a high, mysterious religion bound up with a whole sequence of noble thoughts and feelings — something one could do more than simply believe because told to; something one could love.

Kitty did not arrive at all this through words. Madame Stahl spoke to Kitty as one speaks to a charming child whom one watches with pleasure, the way one looks at a memory of one's own youth; only once, in passing, did she say that in all human sorrows nothing brings comfort but love and faith, and that in the light of Christ's compassion for us no sorrow is small — and at once she turned to other matters. But in every gesture of Madame Stahl, in every word, in every heavenly — as Kitty called it — look, and above all in the whole story of her life, which she heard from Varenka, Kitty recognized that something "important" of which, until now, she had known nothing.

Yet, elevated as Madame Stahl's character was, touching as her story was, and exalted and moving as her speech was, Kitty couldn't help noticing certain traits in her that bothered her. She noticed that when asked about her family, Madame Stahl had smiled with contempt, which did not fit with Christian meekness. She noticed too that when a Catholic priest had been with her, Madame Stahl had carefully kept her face in the shadow of the lamp-shade and had smiled in a peculiar way. Trivial as these two observations were, they unsettled Kitty, and she began to have her doubts about Madame Stahl. But Varenka, on the other hand — alone in the world, without friends or relations, asking nothing, regretting nothing — was exactly the kind of perfection Kitty hardly dared dream of. In Varenka she saw clearly that one had only to forget oneself and love others and one would be calm, happy, and noble. And that was what Kitty longed to be. Now that she could see plainly what was _the most important_, Kitty was not content with merely admiring it; she at once gave herself, with her whole soul, to the new life opening up before her. From Varenka's stories about Madame Stahl and other people she mentioned, Kitty had already drawn up the plan of her own future. She would, like Madame Stahl's niece Aline, of whom Varenka had told her a great deal, seek out the suffering wherever she happened to be living, help them as much as she could, give them the Gospel, read the Gospel to the sick, to criminals, to the dying. The idea of reading the Gospel to criminals, as Aline did, especially fascinated Kitty. But all this stayed secret; she did not speak of it either to her mother or to Varenka.

While she waited for the time when she could carry out her plans on a large scale, however, Kitty even now, at the springs where there were so many sick and unhappy people, easily found chances to practice her new principles in the same way Varenka did.

At first the princess noticed nothing beyond the fact that Kitty was under the strong influence of her _engouement_, as she called it, for Madame Stahl, and still more for Varenka. She saw that Kitty did not just imitate Varenka in her behavior, but unconsciously imitated her way of walking, of talking, of blinking her eyes. But later the princess began to see that, apart from this hero-worship, some real spiritual change was taking place in her daughter.

The princess saw that in the evenings Kitty read a French testament Madame Stahl had given her — something she had never done before; that she avoided her social acquaintances and spent her time with the sick people under Varenka's care, and especially with one poor family, that of a sick painter named Petrov. Kitty was unmistakably proud of playing the part of sister of mercy in that family. All of which was well enough, and the princess had nothing against it, the more so as Petrov's wife was a perfectly decent woman and the German princess, noticing Kitty's devotion, praised her and called her an angel of consolation. All of which would have been fine, if there hadn't been so much excess in it. But the princess could see that her daughter was rushing into extremes, and so she said so to her.
"_Il ne faut jamais rien outrer_," she told her.

Her daughter said nothing in reply; in her heart she was thinking that one couldn't really speak of excess where Christianity was concerned. What excess could there be in practicing a teaching that told you to turn the other cheek when struck, and to hand over your cloak if your coat were taken? But the princess didn't like this excess, and she liked even less the fact that she could feel her daughter was unwilling to open all of her heart to her. Kitty did indeed hide her new views and feelings from her mother. She hid them not because she didn't respect or love her mother, but simply because her mother was her mother. She would have shown them to anyone before her own mother.
"How is it Anna Pavlovna hasn't been to see us for so long?" the princess remarked one day of Madame Petrova. "I've asked her, but she seems put out about something."
"No, I haven't noticed it, maman," said Kitty, flushing hotly.
"Is it long since you went to see them?"
"We're planning a trip to the mountains tomorrow," Kitty answered.
"Well, you can go," the princess said, watching her daughter's embarrassed face and trying to work out what was behind that embarrassment.
That day Varenka came to dinner and reported that Anna Pavlovna had changed her mind and dropped the plan for the next day. And the princess noticed once again that Kitty colored.
"Kitty, haven't you fallen out with the Petrovs about something?" the princess asked when they were alone together. "Why has she stopped sending the children, and stopped coming herself?"

Kitty answered that nothing had happened between them, and that she couldn't say why Anna Pavlovna seemed displeased with her. Kitty answered with complete honesty. She didn't know the reason for the change in Anna Pavlovna, but she could guess at it. She could guess at something she could not tell her mother, something she could not even put into words to herself. It was one of those things one knows but can never say aloud, even to oneself, because to be wrong about it would be too dreadful and too shameful.

Again and again she went over in her memory everything that had happened with that family. She remembered the simple delight on Anna Pavlovna's round, good-humored face when they met; she remembered their quiet councils about the invalid, their little plots to draw him away from the work that was forbidden him and to get him out of doors; the devotion of the youngest boy, who used to call her "my Kitty" and would not go to bed without her. How nice it all had been! Then she pictured Petrov's thin, terribly thin figure, his long neck, the brown coat, the scant curly hair, the questioning blue eyes that had been so frightening to her at first, and his painful attempts to seem hearty and lively in her presence. She remembered the effort she had made at first to overcome the revulsion she felt for him, as for all consumptives, and the trouble it had cost her just to find things to say to him. She remembered the timid, softened way he looked at her, and the strange mix of pity, awkwardness, and later of a sense of her own goodness, that the look had stirred in her. How nice it all had been! But all that was before. Now, a few days ago, everything had suddenly soured. Anna Pavlovna had greeted Kitty with a forced cordiality, and had been watching her and her husband nonstop.
Could that touching pleasure he showed when she came near really be the cause of Anna Pavlovna's coldness?

"Yes," she thought it through, "there was something unnatural in Anna Pavlovna, something utterly unlike her good nature, when she said angrily the day before yesterday, 'There — he'll keep waiting for you; he wouldn't drink his coffee without you, even though he's grown so dreadfully weak.'"

"Yes, perhaps she didn't like it either when I gave him the rug. It was such a simple thing, but he took it so awkwardly, and went on and on thanking me, until I felt awkward myself. And then that portrait of me he did so well. And most of all that look of confusion and tenderness! Yes, yes, that's it!" Kitty repeated to herself in horror. "No, it can't be, it mustn't be! He's so much to be pitied!" she said to herself a moment later.
This doubt poisoned the charm of her new life.

title: Chapter 34
paragraphs: Before the course of taking the waters was over, Prince Shtcherbatsky — who had gone on from Carlsbad to Baden and Kissingen to look up Russian friends, to get a breath of Russian air, as he put it — came back to his wife and daughter.

The prince and princess took completely opposite views of life abroad. The princess thought everything was charming, and despite her settled standing in Russian society she tried, abroad, to play the European fashionable lady — which she wasn't, for the simple reason that she was a thoroughly Russian gentlewoman; so she came across as affected, which didn't quite suit her. The prince, on the contrary, found everything foreign loathsome, was sick of European life, clung to his Russian habits, and went out of his way to seem less European abroad than he really was.

The prince came back thinner, the skin hanging in loose pouches on his cheeks, but in the highest of spirits. His good humor grew even greater when he saw Kitty completely recovered. The news of Kitty's friendship with Madame Stahl and Varenka, and what the princess told him about some change she had noticed in Kitty, troubled him and stirred up his habitual jealousy of anything that drew his daughter away from him, his old fear that she might have slipped out of his reach into regions he could not enter. But these unpleasant feelings were drowned, as always, in the sea of kindness and good humor that was always in him — and more so than ever after his Carlsbad cure.

The day after his arrival, the prince — in his long overcoat, with his Russian wrinkles and baggy cheeks propped up by a starched collar — set off with his daughter to the springs in the brightest possible mood.

It was a lovely morning: the bright, cheerful houses with their little gardens, the sight of the red-faced, red-armed, beer-drinking German waitresses working away merrily, did the heart good. But the closer they got to the springs, the more often they passed sick people, and these looked more pitiable than ever against the everyday prosperity of German life. Kitty no longer felt the contrast. The bright sun, the dazzling green of the foliage, the strains of music were for her the natural setting of all these familiar faces, whose deepening emaciation or signs of recovery she had been watching. But to the prince the brightness and gaiety of the June morning, and the sound of the orchestra playing a fashionable waltz, and above all the look of the healthy attendants, seemed obscene and monstrous when set beside these slowly shuffling, dying figures gathered together from all over Europe. With his favorite daughter on his arm, and even with the feeling of pride and almost of recovered youth that came with it, he felt awkward — almost ashamed — of his brisk step and his sturdy, stout limbs. He felt almost like a man who had forgotten his clothes in a crowd.

"Introduce me to your new friends," he said to his daughter, pressing her hand with his elbow. "I even like your horrid Soden for making you well again. Only it's gloomy here, very gloomy. Who's that?"

Kitty named all the people they met, some of whom she knew and some not. At the garden entrance they ran into the blind lady, Madame Berthe, with her guide, and the prince was delighted to see the old Frenchwoman's face light up at the sound of Kitty's voice. She at once started talking to him with French exaggerated politeness, congratulating him on having such a charming daughter, praising Kitty to the skies right in front of her, calling her a treasure, a pearl, a consoling angel.
"Well, then she's the second angel," the prince said, smiling. "She calls Mademoiselle Varenka angel number one."
"Oh! Mademoiselle Varenka, she really is an angel, allez," Madame Berthe agreed.
In the arcade they met Varenka herself. She was walking briskly toward them, carrying an elegant red bag.
"Here's papa, come at last," Kitty said to her.

Varenka made — simply and naturally, as she did everything — a gesture somewhere between a bow and a curtsey, and at once began speaking to the prince without shyness, naturally, the way she spoke to everyone.
"Of course I know you; I know you very well," the prince said to her with a smile, in which Kitty was glad to detect that her father liked her friend. "Where are you off to in such a hurry?"
"Maman is here," she said, turning to Kitty. "She hasn't slept all night, and the doctor told her to go outside. I'm taking her her work."
"So that's angel number one?" said the prince, when Varenka had gone on.
Kitty could see that her father had meant to make fun of Varenka but couldn't, because he liked her.
"Come on, then, we'll see all your friends," he went on, "even Madame Stahl, if she's willing to recognize me."
"Why, did you know her, papa?" Kitty asked anxiously, catching the glint of irony that lit up in the prince's eyes at the name of Madame Stahl.
"I used to know her husband, and her a little too, before she went over to the Pietists."
"What's a Pietist, papa?" Kitty asked, dismayed to discover that what she so prized in Madame Stahl had a name attached to it.
"I don't quite know myself. I only know that she thanks God for everything, for every misfortune, and even thanks God that her husband died. Which is rather funny, since they didn't get on at all."

"Who's that? What a piteous face!" he asked, spotting a sick man of medium height sitting on a bench, wearing a brown overcoat and white trousers that hung in odd folds about his long, fleshless legs. The man lifted his straw hat to show his scanty curly hair and a high forehead that was painfully red from the press of the hat.

"That's Petrov, an artist," Kitty answered, blushing. "And that's his wife," she added, pointing to Anna Pavlovna, who, as though on cue, at the very moment they came near, moved off after a child that had run down a path.
"Poor man! And what a nice face he has!" said the prince. "Why don't you go up to him? He wanted to speak to you."
"Well, then let's go," said Kitty, turning around resolutely. "How are you feeling today?" she asked Petrov.
Petrov got up, leaning on his stick, and looked shyly at the prince.
"This is my daughter," the prince said. "Allow me to introduce myself."
The painter bowed and smiled, showing his strangely dazzling white teeth.
"We were expecting you yesterday, princess," he said to Kitty. He staggered as he said it, then repeated the movement on purpose, trying to pass it off as deliberate.
"I meant to come, but Varenka said Anna Pavlovna had sent word that you weren't going."
"Not going!" said Petrov, blushing and at once starting to cough, his eyes searching for his wife. "Anita! Anita!" he called loudly, and the swollen veins stood out like cords on his thin white neck.
Anna Pavlovna came over.
"So you sent word to the princess that we weren't going!" he whispered to her angrily, his voice giving out.
"Good morning, princess," said Anna Pavlovna, with a forced smile utterly unlike her former manner. "Very pleased to meet you," she said to the prince. "You've been long expected, prince."

"What did you send word to the princess that we weren't going for?" the artist whispered hoarsely again, even more angrily, plainly furious that his voice failed him and he couldn't put into his words the force he wanted.
"Oh, mercy on us! I thought we weren't going," his wife answered crossly.
"What, when —" He coughed and waved his hand. The prince raised his hat and moved off with his daughter.
"Ah, ah!" he sighed deeply. "Oh, poor things!"

"Yes, papa," Kitty answered. "And you should know they have three children, no servant, and almost no income. He gets something from the Academy," she went on quickly, trying to drown out the distress that Anna Pavlovna's strange change of manner had stirred in her.

"Oh, here's Madame Stahl," said Kitty, pointing to an invalid carriage, in which, propped on pillows, something in gray and blue was lying under a sunshade. This was Madame Stahl. Behind her stood the gloomy, healthy-looking German workman who pushed the carriage. Close by stood a flaxen-haired Swedish count whom Kitty knew by name. Several invalids were lingering near the low carriage, staring at the lady as if she were a curiosity.

The prince walked up to her, and Kitty caught again that disconcerting glint of irony in his eyes. He went up to Madame Stahl and addressed her with extreme courtesy and warmth, in that excellent French so few people speak nowadays.
"I don't know if you remember me, but I must remind you of myself, so that I can thank you for your kindness to my daughter," he said, lifting his hat and not putting it on again.
"Prince Alexander Shtcherbatsky," said Madame Stahl, raising onto him her heavenly eyes, in which Kitty caught a hint of annoyance. "Delighted! I have grown very fond of your daughter."
"You are still in poor health?"
"Yes; I'm used to it," said Madame Stahl, and she introduced the prince to the Swedish count.
"You've hardly changed at all," the prince said to her. "It's been ten or eleven years since I had the honor of seeing you."

"Yes; God sends the cross and sends the strength to bear it. Sometimes one wonders what the point of this life can be? — The other side!" she said sharply to Varenka, who had rearranged the rug over her feet in a way she didn't like.
"To do good, presumably," said the prince with a twinkle in his eye.

"That isn't for us to judge," Madame Stahl said, catching the shade of expression on the prince's face. "So you'll send me that book, dear count? I'm very grateful to you," she said to the young Swede.
"Ah!" cried the prince, catching sight of the Moscow colonel standing nearby, and with a bow to Madame Stahl he moved off with his daughter and the Moscow colonel, who joined them.
"There's our aristocracy for you, prince!" the Moscow colonel said with pointed irony. He nursed a grudge against Madame Stahl for not making his acquaintance.
"She's just the same," the prince replied.
"Did you know her before her illness, prince — that is, before she took to her bed?"
"Yes. She took to her bed right in front of me," said the prince.
"They say it's been ten years since she stood on her feet."
"She doesn't stand up because her legs are too short. She has a very bad figure."
"Papa, that can't be!" cried Kitty.
"That's what wicked tongues say, my dear. And your Varenka catches it too," he added. "Oh, these invalid ladies!"
"Oh, no, papa!" Kitty protested warmly. "Varenka worships her. And she does so much good! Ask anyone! Everyone knows her and Aline Stahl."
"Perhaps," said the prince, squeezing her hand with his elbow; "but it's better when one does good in a way that you can ask everyone and no one knows."

Kitty did not reply, not because she had nothing to say, but because she had no wish to share even with her father what she was really thinking. But, strange to say, although she had so resolved not to let her father's view influence her, not to let him into her inner sanctuary, she felt that the heavenly image of Madame Stahl, which she had carried in her heart for a whole month, had vanished and would not come back — the way a fantastic figure made of clothes thrown down at random vanishes the instant you see it is just a garment lying there. What was left was a woman with short legs, who lay down because her figure was bad, and who badgered patient Varenka about the rug. And no effort of imagination could bring the former Madame Stahl back to Kitty.

title: Chapter 35
paragraphs: The prince's good humor spread through his own family and their friends, and even to the German landlord in whose rooms the Shtcherbatskys were staying.

Coming back from the springs with Kitty, the prince — having invited the colonel and Marya Yevgenyevna and Varenka over for coffee — gave orders for a table and chairs to be carried into the garden under the chestnut tree, and for lunch to be laid there. The landlord and the servants also caught his bright spirits. They knew how generous he was; and half an hour later the invalid doctor from Hamburg, who lived on the top floor, was looking enviously out of his window at the cheerful party of healthy Russians gathered under the chestnut tree. In the trembling circles of shadow thrown by the leaves, at a table covered with a white cloth and laid with a coffee pot, bread and butter, cheese and cold game, sat the princess in a high cap with lilac ribbons, handing round cups and bread and butter. At the other end sat the prince, eating heartily and talking loudly and merrily. The prince had laid out beside him his various purchases — carved boxes, knickknacks, paper knives of every kind, of which he bought a heap at every spa — and was giving them away to everyone, including Lieschen the servant girl and the landlord, with whom he joked in his comically bad German, insisting that it wasn't the water that had cured Kitty, but his splendid cooking, and especially his plum soup. The princess laughed at her husband for his Russian ways, but she was livelier and more good-humored than she had been the whole time at the waters. The colonel smiled, as always, at the prince's jokes, but on the subject of Europe — which he believed himself to be studying carefully — he took the princess's side. The simple-hearted Marya Yevgenyevna simply howled with laughter at every absurd thing the prince said, and his jokes left Varenka helpless with that feeble but infectious laughter Kitty had never seen in her before.

All of this pleased Kitty, but she could not be light-hearted herself. She couldn't solve the problem her father had unwittingly set her by his good-humored view of her friends and of the life that had so drawn her in. To that doubt was added the change in her relations with the Petrovs, which had been so glaring and so unpleasant that very morning. Everyone was in good spirits, but Kitty could not be, and that only deepened her distress. She felt the way she had as a child when she had been shut up in her room as punishment and had heard her sisters' cheerful laughter outside.
"Well, what did you buy this mountain of things for?" the princess asked, smiling, as she handed her husband a cup of coffee.
"You go for a walk, you stop in at a shop, and they ask you to buy. '_Erlaucht, Durchlaucht?_' The moment they say '_Durchlaucht_,' I can't hold out. I lose ten thalers."
"It's pure boredom," said the princess.
"Of course it is. Such boredom, my dear, that one doesn't know what to do with oneself."
"How can you be bored, prince? There's so much that's interesting in Germany now," said Marya Yevgenyevna.
"But I know all the interesting things: the plum soup I know, the pea sausages I know. I know everything."
"No, say what you like, prince — there's interest in their institutions," said the colonel.

"What's interesting about it? They're all as pleased with themselves as brass farthings. They've conquered everybody, and why am I supposed to be pleased about that? I haven't conquered anyone; meanwhile I'm forced to take off my own boots, yes, and put them away too; get up in the morning, dress at once, and head for the dining room to drink bad tea! How different at home! You get up at your own pace, you grumble a little, come round again. You have time to think things over, no rush."
"But time is money, you forget that," said the colonel.
"Time, indeed — that depends! There's time you'd give a month of for sixpence, and time you wouldn't give half an hour of for any money. Isn't that so, Katinka? What's wrong? Why are you so glum?"
"I'm not glum."
"Where are you off to? Stay a little longer," he said to Varenka.
"I need to be getting home," Varenka said, standing up, and once more she dissolved into a giggle. When she had recovered, she said goodbye and went into the house to fetch her hat.
Kitty followed her. Even Varenka looked different to her now. Not worse — just different from what she had imagined her to be.
"Oh, dear, it's been ages since I laughed so much!" Varenka said, gathering up her parasol and her bag. "How nice he is, your father!"
Kitty said nothing.
"When will I see you again?" Varenka asked.
"Mamma was meaning to go and see the Petrovs. Won't you be there?" said Kitty, testing Varenka.
"Yes," Varenka answered. "They're getting ready to leave, so I promised to help them pack."
"Well, I'll come too, then."
"No, why should you?"
"Why not? Why not? Why not?" Kitty said, opening her eyes wide and grabbing at Varenka's parasol so as not to let her go. "No, wait — why not?"
"Oh, nothing; your father has come, and besides, they'll feel awkward at your helping."
"No, tell me why you don't want me at the Petrovs' often. You don't want me to — why not?"
"I didn't say that," Varenka said quietly.
"No, please tell me!"
"Tell you everything?" Varenka asked.
"Everything, everything!" Kitty agreed.

"Well, there's nothing of any real consequence; only that Mihail Alexeyevitch" — that was the painter's name — "had been meaning to leave earlier, and now he doesn't want to go," Varenka said, smiling.
"Well, well!" Kitty pressed her impatiently, glaring at Varenka.

"Well, for some reason Anna Pavlovna told him that he doesn't want to go because you're here. Of course it was nonsense; but there was a row about it — about you. You know how irritable these sick people are."
Kitty, scowling worse than ever, kept silent, and Varenka went on talking on her own, trying to soften the blow, seeing a storm coming — though she didn't know whether of tears or of words.
"So you'd better not go. You understand? You won't be offended?"
"And it serves me right! It serves me right!" Kitty cried at once, snatching the parasol out of Varenka's hand, looking past her friend's face.
Varenka felt like smiling at her childish fury, but was afraid of wounding her.
"How does it serve you right? I don't understand," she said.

"It serves me right, because the whole thing was sham; because the whole thing was done deliberately and not from the heart. What business had I meddling in strangers' lives? And so here I am, the cause of a quarrel, and I've done what no one ever asked me to do. Because it was all a sham! A sham! A sham!"
"A sham? With what object?" Varenka asked gently.
"Oh, it's so stupid, so hateful! There was no need for any of it on my part. Nothing but sham!" she said, opening and shutting the parasol.
"But with what object?"
"To look better in everyone's eyes, in my own, in God's; to deceive everyone. No, I won't stoop to that any more. I'll be bad — but at any rate not a liar, not a cheat."
"But who's a cheat?" said Varenka reproachfully. "You speak as if —"
But Kitty was in one of her gusts of fury, and wouldn't let her finish.

"I'm not talking about you — not about you at all. You are perfection. Yes, yes, I know you're all perfection; but what am I to do if I'm bad? None of this would have happened if I weren't bad. So let me be what I am. I won't be a sham. What have I to do with Anna Pavlovna? Let them go their way and let me go mine. I can't be any other way. And yet that's not it — that's not it either."
"What isn't it?" Varenka asked, baffled.
"Any of it. I can't act except from the heart, and you act from principle. I liked you simply — but you most likely only wanted to save me, to improve me."
"You are being unjust," Varenka said.
"But I'm not talking about other people, I'm talking about myself."
"Kitty," came her mother's voice, "come here, show papa your necklace."
Kitty, with a haughty air, without making peace with her friend, took the necklace in its little box from the table and went to her mother.
"What's the matter? Why are you so red?" both her mother and father asked at the same moment.
"Nothing," she said. "I'll be back in a minute," and she ran back.

"She's still here," she thought. "What am I going to say to her? Oh, dear — what have I done, what have I said? Why was I rude to her? What am I to do? What am I to say to her?" Kitty thought, and she stopped in the doorway.
Varenka in her hat, parasol in her hands, was sitting at the table examining the spring Kitty had broken. She raised her head.
"Varenka, forgive me — please, forgive me," Kitty whispered, going up to her. "I don't even remember what I said. I —"
"I really didn't mean to hurt you," Varenka said, smiling.

Peace was made. But with her father's arrival the whole world Kitty had been living in had been transformed. She did not throw out all she had learned, but she had to admit she had deceived herself in thinking she could be what she had wanted to be. Her eyes were opened, as it were; she felt how hard it was to keep herself, free from hypocrisy and self-conceit, on the heights she had hoped to climb to. Beyond that, she felt the dreariness of the world of suffering, of sick and dying people, in which she had been moving. The effort she had been making to like it now seemed unbearable to her, and she longed to get back quickly into fresh air, to Russia, to Ergushovo, where, as she knew from letters, her sister Dolly had already gone with her children.
But her affection for Varenka didn't fade. Saying goodbye, Kitty begged her to come to them in Russia.
"I'll come when you get married," Varenka said.
"I shall never marry."
"Well, then, I shall never come."
