"Well, then, I'll get married just for that. Now mind — remember your promise," Kitty said.
The doctor's prediction came true. Kitty went home to Russia cured. She was no longer as gay and thoughtless as before, but she was at peace. Her Moscow troubles had become a memory.
PART THREE

title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: Sergey Ivanovitch Koznishev wanted a rest from intellectual work, and instead of going abroad as he usually did, he came toward the end of May to stay in the country with his brother. In his judgment, country life was the best kind of life. He had come now to enjoy that life at his brother's. Konstantin Levin was very glad of his company, especially since he had not been expecting his brother Nikolay that summer. But for all his affection and respect for Sergey Ivanovitch, Konstantin Levin felt awkward with his brother in the country. He felt awkward, and even positively annoyed, by his brother's attitude toward country life. For Konstantin Levin the country was the ground of life itself — of its pleasures, its struggles, its labor. For Sergey Ivanovitch the country meant, on one hand, a rest from work, and on the other hand a valuable antidote to the corrupting influences of town, which he took with satisfaction and a sense of its usefulness. For Konstantin Levin the country was good first of all because it offered a field for labor whose usefulness was beyond question. For Sergey Ivanovitch the country was particularly fine because there one could, and was entitled to, do nothing. What was more, Sergey Ivanovitch's attitude toward the peasants got under Konstantin's skin. Sergey Ivanovitch was fond of saying he knew and liked the peasantry, and he often talked with peasants — which he knew how to do without affectation or condescension — and from every such conversation he would draw broad conclusions in favor of the peasantry and as proof that he understood them. Konstantin Levin did not like this kind of attitude toward the peasants. For Konstantin a peasant was simply the chief partner in their shared labor, and despite all the respect and the love — almost like kinship — he felt for the peasant (sucked in, as he said himself, with the milk of his peasant nurse), still, as a fellow worker, while he sometimes admired the strength, gentleness, and fairness of these men, he was just as often, when the work demanded other qualities, exasperated with the peasant for his carelessness, lack of method, drunkenness, and lying. If anyone had asked him whether he liked or disliked the peasants, Konstantin Levin would have been utterly at a loss for an answer. He liked them and didn't like them, just as he liked and didn't like men in general. Being a good-natured man, of course, he liked men more than he disliked them, and the same with the peasants. But to like or dislike "the people" as something separate he simply couldn't, not only because he lived with "the people" and all his interests were tied up with theirs, but also because he saw himself as part of "the people," couldn't see any special virtues or failings setting himself apart from them, and couldn't set himself against them. What was more, although he had lived in the closest contact with the peasants for years — as farmer, as arbitrator, and above all as adviser (the peasants trusted him, and for thirty miles around they would come to him for counsel) — he had no settled view of "the people," and would have been just as stumped to answer whether he knew "the people" as whether he liked them. For him to claim he knew the peasantry would have been the same as claiming to know men. He was constantly watching and getting to know people of all kinds, peasants among them, whom he saw as good and interesting people, and he was constantly finding new things in them, altering his old views of them and forming new ones. With Sergey Ivanovitch it was just the opposite. Just as he liked and praised country life by contrast with the life he didn't like, so he liked the peasantry by contrast with the class of men he didn't like, and so he knew the peasantry as something distinct from and opposed to men generally. In his methodical mind certain features of peasant life were sharply defined, deduced partly from peasant life itself but mostly from the contrast with other ways of life. He never changed his opinion of the peasantry or his sympathetic attitude toward them.

In the arguments that came up between the brothers about their views of the peasantry, Sergey Ivanovitch always got the better of his brother, precisely because Sergey Ivanovitch had a definite idea of the peasant — his character, his qualities, his tastes. Konstantin Levin had no fixed and unchanging view on the subject, so in their arguments Konstantin was easily caught contradicting himself.

In Sergey Ivanovitch's eyes his younger brother was a fine fellow, _with his heart in the right place_ (as he put it in French), but with a mind that, though quick enough, was too easily swayed by the impressions of the moment and so was full of contradictions. With all the condescension of an older brother he would sometimes explain to him what things really meant, but he got little satisfaction out of arguing with him, because the victories came too easily.

Konstantin Levin saw his brother as a man of immense intellect and culture, generous in the highest sense of the word, and gifted with a special capacity for work in the public good. But in the bottom of his heart, the older he grew and the more closely he knew his brother, the more often the thought struck him that this capacity for work in the public good — of which he felt himself entirely lacking — might not really be a quality at all, but a lack of something. Not a lack of good, honest, noble desires and tastes, but a lack of vital force, of what is called heart — the impulse that drives a man to choose one path out of all the countless paths of life and to care only about that one. The better he knew his brother, the more he noticed that Sergey Ivanovitch, and many of the others who worked for the public welfare, were not led by any impulse of the heart to care about the public good, but reasoned out from intellectual considerations that it was the right thing to take interest in public affairs, and so took interest in them. Levin was confirmed in this generalization by the fact that his brother took questions of the public welfare or of the immortality of the soul no more to heart than chess problems or the ingenious design of a new machine.

On top of all that, Konstantin Levin was not at ease with his brother because in summer in the country Levin was busy with farm work all the time, and the long summer day was not long enough for everything he had to do, while Sergey Ivanovitch was taking a holiday. But although he was on holiday now — that is, he was doing no writing — he was so used to intellectual activity that he liked to put the ideas that occurred to him into a clean, polished form, and liked to have someone to listen. His most usual and natural listener was his brother. So, despite the warmth and directness of their relations, Konstantin felt awkward leaving him alone. Sergey Ivanovitch liked to stretch out on the grass in the sun and lie there, basking and chatting lazily.
"You'd never believe," he would tell his brother, "how this rural idleness delights me. Not a thought in one's head — empty as a drum!"

But Konstantin Levin found it dull to sit and listen to him, especially when he knew that while he was away they would be carting dung onto fields that hadn't been ploughed for it, and piling it up any way they liked; that they wouldn't screw the shares into the ploughs, and would let them come off, and then say the new ploughs were a silly invention and nothing beat the old Andreevna plough, and so on.
"Come on — you've done enough tramping about in the heat," Sergey Ivanovitch would say to him.
"No, I just need to run round to the counting house for a minute," Levin would answer, and off he'd go to the fields.

paragraphs: Early in June it happened that Agafea Mihalovna, the old nurse and housekeeper, slipped while carrying a jar of mushrooms she had just pickled down to the cellar, fell, and sprained her wrist. The district doctor, a talkative young medical student who had just finished his training, came to see her. He examined the wrist, declared it wasn't broken, was delighted at the chance to talk with the famous Sergey Ivanovitch Koznishev, and, to show off his progressive views, told him all the scandals of the district and complained of the wretched state the district council had fallen into. Sergey Ivanovitch listened attentively, asked questions, and, drawn out by a new listener, talked fluently, dropped a few sharp and weighty remarks, respectfully appreciated by the young doctor, and was soon in that eager state of mind his brother knew so well — the one that always came over him after a brilliant, animated conversation. After the doctor left, he wanted to take a fishing rod down to the river. Sergey Ivanovitch was fond of angling, and seemed almost proud of being able to take an interest in so foolish an occupation.
Konstantin Levin, whose presence was needed in the ploughland and the meadows, had come with the trap to pick his brother up.

It was that turning-point of summer when the year's crop is a certainty, when one starts thinking about the sowing for the next year, and the mowing is at hand; when the rye is all in ear, though the ears are still light and not yet full, and waves in gray-green billows in the wind; when the green oats, with tufts of yellow grass scattered through them here and there, droop unevenly over the late-sown fields; when the early buckwheat is already out and hiding the ground; when the fallow lands, beaten hard as stone by the cattle, are half ploughed up with paths still untouched by the plough; when from the dry dung heaps carted out onto the fields at sunset comes a smell of manure mixed with meadowsweet; and when down in the lowlands the riverside meadows are a thick sea of grass waiting to be mown, with blackened heaps of sorrel stalks scattered through it.

It was that brief lull in the work of the fields, just before the start of the harvest labors — labors that come round year after year, year after year stretching every nerve of the peasants. The crop was splendid, and bright hot summer days had set in, with short, dewy nights.

The brothers had to drive through the woods to reach the meadows. Sergey Ivanovitch was admiring the beauty of the woods the whole way — a tangled mass of leaves — pointing out to his brother now an old lime tree about to flower, dark on its shady side and brightly speckled with yellow stipules, now the year's young saplings brilliant with emerald. Konstantin Levin did not enjoy talking or hearing about the beauty of nature. Words, for him, drained the beauty out of what he saw. He agreed with what his brother said, but he could not help his thoughts drifting to other matters. When they came out of the woods, his attention was caught entirely by the view of the fallow on the upland, yellow in places with grass, in places trampled and seamed with furrows, in places dotted with ridges of dung, in places already ploughed. A string of carts was moving across it. Levin counted the carts and was pleased to see that all the carts he needed had been brought, and at the sight of the meadows his thoughts turned to the mowing. There was always something about haymaking that touched him to the quick. When they reached the meadow, Levin stopped the horse.

The morning dew was still lying on the thick undergrowth of grass, and so that he wouldn't get his feet wet, Sergey Ivanovitch asked his brother to drive him in the trap up to the willow from which carp were caught. As sorry as Konstantin Levin was to crush down his own mowing grass, he drove him into the meadow. The high grass turned softly around the wheels and the horse's legs, leaving its seeds clinging to the wet axles and spokes. His brother settled himself under a bush, sorting out his tackle, while Levin led the horse away, fastened him up, and walked into the vast gray-green sea of grass, motionless in the windless air. The silky grass, with its ripe seed, came almost up to his waist in the wettest spots.
Crossing the meadow, Konstantin Levin came out onto the road and met an old man with a swollen eye, carrying a skep on his shoulder.
"What, picked up a stray swarm, Fomitch?" he asked.

"No, indeed, Konstantin Dmitrich! All we can do to hold onto our own! This is the second swarm that's flown away. Lucky the lads caught them. They were ploughing your field. They unyoked the horses and tore after them."
"Well, what do you say, Fomitch — start the mowing, or wait a bit?"
"Eh, well. Our way is to wait till St. Peter's Day. But you always mow earlier. Well, sure enough, please God, the hay is good. There'll be plenty for the beasts."
"What do you think about the weather?"
"That's in God's hands. Maybe it'll hold fine."
Levin went over to his brother.

Sergey Ivanovitch had caught nothing, but he wasn't bored, and seemed in the cheerfullest of moods. Levin could see that, fired up by his talk with the doctor, he wanted to talk on. Levin himself, on the other hand, would have liked to get home as quickly as possible, so as to give the orders for gathering the mowers for the next day and to settle the doubts about the mowing that were eating at him.
"Well, let's be off," he said.

"Why be in such a rush? Let's stay a bit. But look how wet you are! Even if you catch nothing, it's still pleasant. That's the best thing about every kind of sport — that one is dealing with nature. Look at this steely water — how lovely it is!" said Sergey Ivanovitch. "These riverbanks always remind me of the riddle — do you know it? 'The grass says to the water: we shiver and we shiver.'"
"I don't know the riddle," Levin answered wearily.
